item.content:encoded:
Laylat al-Qadr 2027 is expected to fall on one of the odd nights in the last ten nights of Ramadan 1448. Ramadan is expected to begin on about 8 February 2027, which puts the first of those ten nights on the evening of about 27 February. Nobody knows the exact night, and that is part of the gift: it invites you to give the whole stretch your attention.

Here are the odd nights with their expected evenings. Remember that an Islamic night begins at sunset, so each night starts the evening before its day.

  • 21st night: expected evening of about 27 February 2027
  • 23rd night: expected evening of about 1 March 2027
  • 25th night: expected evening of about 3 March 2027
  • 27th night: expected evening of about 5 March 2027
  • 29th night: expected evening of about 7 March 2027

All of these dates are expected, not confirmed. Ramadan starts with local moon sighting or your local authority’s announcement, so your night may shift by a day.

What is Laylat al-Qadr?

Laylat al-Qadr is often translated as the Night of Decree or the Night of Power. It is the night on which the Qur’an began to be revealed, and the Qur’an gives it a weight no other night has.

Surah Al-Qadr (chapter 97) tells us that the Night of Decree is better than a thousand months. A thousand months is more than 83 years, so one night of sincere worship can outweigh a full lifetime of ordinary nights.

Surah Ad-Dukhan (44:3) also refers to the night, describing it as a blessed night on which the Qur’an was sent down.

For the reader, the point is practical. You do not need special knowledge or a perfect record to use this night. You need to show up with sincerity and make the most of the time you have.

Which night is Laylat al-Qadr?

The Prophet (peace be upon him) told the believers to look for Laylat al-Qadr in the odd nights of the last ten nights of Ramadan.

Many Muslims lean towards the 27th night, and this view has a long history in the Muslim community. It is not the only view. Some scholars have favoured other odd nights, and some have said it can move from year to year. So the 27th night is a strong candidate in the minds of many, and still not a certainty.

Why would the night be left unspecified? Scholars have offered reasons. One often-cited reflection is that a hidden night encourages people to worship across all of the last ten nights instead of one.

If you are asking about the 27th night of Ramadan 2027, the expected evening is about 5 March. If you can only give a few nights real effort, the odd nights are the ones the hadith points to. Giving all ten is better still.

The Laylat al-Qadr dua

The dua most associated with this night comes from a narration of Aisha (may Allah be pleased with her). She asked the Prophet (peace be upon him) what she should say if she found Laylat al-Qadr, and he taught her a short dua for forgiveness.

اللَّهُمَّ إِنَّكَ عَفُوٌّ تُحِبُّ الْعَفْوَ فَاعْفُ عَنِّي

(Sunan Ibn Majah 3850; Jami’ at-Tirmidhi 3513)

Some printings of Tirmidhi add the word karim; the shorter wording above is the one most scholars consider established.

Transliteration: Allahumma innaka ‘afuwwun tuhibbul ‘afwa fa’fu ‘anni

Meaning: O Allah, You are the Pardoner, You love to pardon, so pardon me.

It is short enough to memorise in a few minutes and to repeat in sujood, after prayer or while you walk around the house. You can also add your own du’a in your own language. Many people write a short list beforehand so the important requests do not slip away at 3 a.m.

A simple plan for the last ten nights

You do not need an elaborate schedule. A plan you can keep for ten nights beats a perfect one that lasts two.

Qiyam

Pray extra units at night after Isha, or closer to Fajr if that is when you can stay awake. Even a few rak’ahs counts. If you pray taraweeh, consider staying with the imam until the end.

Qur’an

Set a small, realistic amount and keep to it. A page after each prayer adds up. If you can, include Surah Al-Qadr in your recitation and take a minute to read its meaning.

A du’a list

Write down what you want to ask for: forgiveness, family, health, guidance, people you love who are struggling. Keep the list by your prayer mat. Include the dua above.

Charity

Give something on each night, even if it is small. Setting up a standing donation for the ten nights takes the decision out of a tired evening.

I’tikaf

I’tikaf means staying in the mosque for worship, and many Muslims do it in the last ten days. It has its own conditions, so this article does not cover them. See our separate guide on i’tikaf.

If you work or have young children

The last ten nights do not ask you to be someone else. If you work during the day, choose one fixed slot, such as 30 minutes after Isha, and protect it. If you have young children, split the night with your spouse, or pray your qiyam at home in short turns. Short, regular worship done sincerely is real worship.

Muslims Day can help with the practical side. Its prayer times for Isha and Fajr show you the window for night prayer in your city, and the Duas section keeps your du’as in one place when you need them.

Signs of Laylat al-Qadr mentioned in hadith

People share many signs of Laylat al-Qadr online, and a lot of them have no source. This section sticks to what is reported in the hadith.

One narration describes that the sun rises the following morning without strong rays.

That is the only sign included here, because it is the one our research notes support.

You do not need to see a sign to benefit from the night. Most people will not notice anything unusual. Worship the whole last ten nights, and leave the rest to Allah.

Laylat al-Qadr 2027 FAQ

When is Laylat al-Qadr 2027?

It is expected to fall on one of the odd nights in the last ten nights of Ramadan 2027, with the first of those nights expected on the evening of about 27 February. The exact night is not known.

Is Laylat al-Qadr always on the 27th?

No ruling says so. Many Muslims favour the 27th night, but scholars have also pointed to other odd nights.

What dua should I read on Laylat al-Qadr?

Allahumma innaka ‘afuwwun tuhibbul ‘afwa fa’fu ‘anni, taught by the Prophet (peace be upon him) to Aisha (may Allah be pleased with her).

What are the signs of Laylat al-Qadr?

One reported sign is that the sun rises the next morning without strong rays. Signs are not a condition for receiving the reward.

Can women on their period benefit from Laylat al-Qadr?

The mainstream view is that a woman on her period cannot pray or fast, but she can still make du’a and dhikr, and she can seek the night through them. Scholars differ on details such as reciting the Qur’an.

Get ready for Laylat al-Qadr 2027

Laylat al-Qadr 2027 is months away, and that is a good thing. You have time to choose your nights, write your du’a list and decide what you can keep up. Pick the dua above, learn it, and keep it ready for the evening of about 27 February.

To make the plan easier, set your Isha and Fajr reminders in Muslims Day, add your du’as to the Duas section, and check the Hijri calendar closer to Ramadan as the dates are confirmed.

TL;DR: Key Takeaways

  • Start your Ramadan countdown 100 days early to build lasting habits without rushing.
  • Focus on three areas: spiritual growth, physical health, and financial preparation.
  • Follow a four-phase plan: reset and plan, build habits, stay consistent, and finalize preparations.
  • Strengthen your Salah, Quran recitation, dua, and daily acts of worship gradually.
  • Prepare your sleep schedule, eating habits, and health before Ramadan begins.
  • Create a Ramadan budget for groceries, Zakat, Sadaqah, and Eid expenses.
  • Use a simple checklist to track your progress and stay consistent.
  • Use Muslims Day to support your daily prayer, Quran, dhikr, and worship routine.

Why Start a Ramadan Countdown 100 Days Early?

Ramadan has a way of arriving before we feel ready. One moment, it seems months away. Suddenly, we are planning groceries, adjusting our sleep schedules, setting spiritual goals, and wondering how to make the most of the holiest month of the year.

The problem is not always a lack of intention. Often, it is a lack of preparation.

A Ramadan countdown gives you the opportunity to prepare gradually instead of trying to change everything in the final week. You can strengthen your relationship with Allah, improve your daily routine, organize your finances, and make space for worship before Ramadan begins.

The goal is not to spend 100 days preparing a perfect schedule. It is to enter Ramadan with a stronger foundation and a clearer sense of purpose.

This guide divides your preparation into four practical phases, covering spiritual, physical, and financial readiness. You can start on any day and adapt the plan to your circumstances.

The 100-Day Ramadan Preparation Roadmap

Divide your Ramadan countdown into four manageable phases. Each phase has a different focus, allowing you to build good habits gradually.

Phase 1: Days 100 to 71, Reset and Plan

Use the first 30 days to assess your current habits, set realistic goals, and prepare a practical plan.

  • Reflect on your relationship with Allah and renew your intentions.
  • Identify the worship habits you want to improve.
  • Choose a realistic daily Quran reading target.
  • Review your sleep schedule and eating habits.
  • Assess your income, expenses, savings, and charitable goals.
  • Create a simple checklist for your Ramadan preparation.

Your goal is to finish this phase with a clear plan, not a perfect routine.

Phase 2: Days 70 to 41, Build the Habits

Once you have a plan, begin turning your intentions into daily actions. Focus on building a routine that feels natural rather than forcing yourself into an unrealistic schedule.

  • Work toward praying the five obligatory prayers consistently and on time.
  • Establish a manageable Quran reading routine.
  • Set aside time for dua, dhikr, and seeking forgiveness.
  • Improve your sleep schedule and eating habits gradually.
  • Start saving regularly for Ramadan and Eid expenses.
  • Learn the essential Islamic rules of fasting.

Some Muslims also practice voluntary fasting on Mondays and Thursdays or other recommended days. If you choose to do this, consider your health and personal circumstances. Voluntary fasting is not necessary to complete this preparation plan.

Your goal is to establish a few habits you can maintain even on busy days.

Phase 3: Days 40 to 11, Stay Consistent

This phase is about maintaining the habits you have already developed instead of constantly adding new goals.

  • Review your progress with Salah, Quran recitation, dua, and dhikr.
  • Adjust any habits that feel too difficult to maintain.
  • Continue eating balanced meals and getting adequate sleep.
  • Review your Ramadan savings and expected expenses.
  • Plan affordable meals and prepare a grocery list.
  • Reduce unnecessary distractions and protect time for worship.

Ask yourself whether your preparation is helping you become more consistent. If something is not working, make adjustments rather than abandoning the plan.

Your goal is to protect your progress and remove obstacles before Ramadan begins.

Phase 4: Days 10 to 1, Final Preparation

The final ten days of your countdown are for organizing practical details and preparing mentally for the change in routine.

  • Organize your prayer space and worship essentials.
  • Prepare a realistic daily schedule around local prayer times.
  • Plan simple suhoor and iftar meals.
  • Complete essential shopping early where practical.
  • Review your budget and finalize your charitable plans.
  • Choose three to five meaningful spiritual goals for Ramadan.
  • Check your local Islamic authority for the confirmed start date.

Your goal is to enter Ramadan organized, prepared, and focused on worship.

Spiritual Readiness: Prepare Your Heart for Ramadan

Ramadan is an opportunity to strengthen your relationship with Allah. However, meaningful spiritual preparation does not need to begin with an overwhelming routine.

Start with small, sincere actions and build consistency over time.

1. Strengthen Your Salah

Focus on praying the five obligatory prayers consistently and on time. If you already maintain your prayers, work on understanding their meanings and improving your concentration.

Use the weeks before Ramadan to establish a routine that accommodates your work, studies, and family responsibilities.

2. Build a Daily Quran Habit

You do not need to begin by reading large portions of the Quran every day.

Choose a realistic target, such as a few pages daily. You can also read a translation, study a short surah, or learn about the meaning of the verses you recite.

The objective is to make Quran recitation a consistent part of your life before Ramadan begins.

3. Make Time for Dua and Dhikr

Set aside a few minutes each day to remember Allah, seek forgiveness, and make dua for yourself and others.

You can prepare a list of duas you want to learn or revisit during Ramadan. Gradually building this habit can make your worship more intentional.

4. Learn the Essentials of Fasting

Use your preparation period to understand the basic rules of fasting, what invalidates a fast, and the concessions available to people who cannot fast safely.

If you have questions about your particular circumstances, consult a knowledgeable Islamic scholar.

5. Improve Your Character

Ramadan is not only about abstaining from food and drink. It is also an opportunity to improve patience, honesty, kindness, and self-control.

Start working on one habit you would like to change. This might mean avoiding gossip, managing anger, speaking more thoughtfully, or being more generous toward others.

Physical Readiness: Prepare Your Body for Fasting

Taking care of your physical health can make the transition into Ramadan easier. You do not need an extreme diet or demanding exercise routine. Focus on sustainable improvements.

1. Improve Your Sleep Schedule

If you usually sleep late and wake up late, gradually adjust your schedule before Ramadan.

Establish a consistent bedtime and wake-up time. Preparing in advance can make waking up for suhoor and Fajr less difficult.

2. Develop Healthier Eating Habits

Begin eating balanced meals that include protein, vegetables, fruit, whole grains, and other nutritious foods suited to your needs.

Avoid relying excessively on highly processed foods, sugary snacks, or very heavy meals. Developing balanced eating habits beforehand can help you make better choices during Ramadan.

3. Stay Hydrated

Drink water regularly throughout the day. Once Ramadan begins, you will need to pay attention to hydration between iftar and suhoor.

Individual hydration needs vary according to health, activity, weather, and other factors.

4. Stay Physically Active

Walking and other manageable forms of exercise can help you maintain your energy and general fitness.

Choose an activity that fits your schedule and gradually build consistency. Avoid pushing yourself into an exhausting routine just before Ramadan.

5. Address Existing Health Concerns

If you have a medical condition, take regular medication, or are unsure whether fasting is safe for you, consult your healthcare professional before Ramadan.

Do not stop prescribed medication or make significant treatment changes without medical advice. Islam provides concessions for people who cannot safely fast, and protecting your health is important.

Financial Readiness: Plan Your Ramadan Budget

Ramadan can bring additional expenses, especially when households prepare special meals, organize iftar gatherings, donate to charitable causes, and purchase Eid gifts.

Preparing a budget early can help you manage these expenses without unnecessary financial stress.

1. Review Your Current Finances

Start by reviewing your income, essential expenses, savings, and outstanding financial obligations.

Identify expenses that can be reduced and determine how much you can realistically set aside for Ramadan.

2. Create a Ramadan Savings Fund

Decide on a manageable amount to save regularly. Even small contributions can help cover additional expenses when Ramadan arrives.

Keep essential household costs and financial obligations as your priority.

3. Plan for Zakat and Sadaqah

If Zakat is due on your wealth, learn how to calculate it correctly and determine when it must be paid.

You can also plan voluntary Sadaqah according to your financial circumstances. Consider supporting trustworthy charitable organizations, feeding people in need, or helping struggling families.

Remember that Zakat and voluntary charity have different rules and purposes.

4. Control Grocery and Iftar Expenses

Plan simple meals and prepare a shopping list before purchasing groceries.

Avoid buying more food than your household needs. Planning meals can reduce waste and help you manage your budget more effectively.

5. Prepare for Eid Early

Include clothing, travel, gifts, and other expected Eid expenses in your financial plan.

Setting aside money in advance can help you enjoy the occasion without relying on unnecessary borrowing or last-minute spending.

Your 100-Day Ramadan Preparation Checklist

Use this checklist to review your progress throughout the countdown.

Spiritual Preparation

  • Renew your intention and set clear goals.
  • Build a consistent Salah routine.
  • Establish a daily Quran reading habit.
  • Make time for dua and dhikr.
  • Review the essential rules of fasting.
  • Identify one aspect of your character to improve.

Physical Preparation

  • Improve your sleep schedule gradually.
  • Plan balanced meals and hydration.
  • Build a manageable physical activity routine.
  • Address existing health concerns.
  • Seek medical advice about fasting if needed.

Financial Preparation

  • Create a realistic Ramadan budget.
  • Plan for groceries and household necessities.
  • Calculate Zakat if it is due.
  • Set a reasonable Sadaqah budget.
  • Plan Eid expenses in advance.
  • Reduce unnecessary spending where possible.

Review this checklist weekly. You do not need to complete every item immediately. The goal is to make steady progress and enter Ramadan feeling more prepared.

How to Make Your Ramadan Countdown Successful

A preparation plan works best when it fits your actual life. Use these practical tips to stay on track.

Start Small

Choose manageable actions instead of changing your entire routine at once. A few minutes of Quran recitation every day can be a better starting point than an unrealistic reading target.

Track Progress, Not Perfection

Missing a goal does not mean your preparation has failed. Identify what went wrong, adjust your routine, and start again.

Make Your Environment Supportive

Keep your Quran, prayer mat, and other worship essentials accessible. Organize your schedule and discuss household plans with your family.

Protect Your Rest

Spiritual preparation should not come at the expense of your health. Build a routine that allows enough sleep and time for your daily responsibilities.

Review Your Plan Weekly

Spend a few minutes reviewing what worked, what did not, and what needs to change. Adjust your goals according to your circumstances.

Remember Your Intention

Ramadan preparation is not a productivity competition. Its purpose is to help you worship sincerely, strengthen your relationship with Allah, and become a better Muslim.

Frequently Asked Questions About the Ramadan Countdown

1. When should I start my Ramadan countdown?

Starting 100 days before Ramadan gives you time to develop spiritual habits, improve your routine, and organize your finances. However, you can begin preparing at any time. Even a few days of intentional preparation can be valuable.

2. What should I focus on during the 100-day preparation plan?

Focus on three main areas: spiritual readiness, physical readiness, and financial readiness. Build consistency with Salah and Quran recitation, establish healthy daily routines, and prepare a realistic budget for Ramadan and Eid.

3. Do I need to fast before Ramadan to prepare?

No. Voluntary fasting is an optional act of worship, not a requirement for this preparation plan. You can prepare through prayer, Quran recitation, improving your daily routine, and learning about the rules of fasting.

4. How can I stay consistent throughout the countdown?

Set small, specific goals and review them every week. Use a checklist or an Islamic lifestyle app to organize your routine. If you miss a day, continue from where you left off rather than abandoning your plan.

5. How much money should I save for Ramadan?

There is no single amount suitable for everyone. Your budget depends on your income, household size, regular expenses, and charitable obligations. Estimate essential costs first, then decide what you can reasonably save for charity and Eid.

6. What if I have less than 100 days left?

Do not worry about completing every phase. Identify your most important spiritual, physical, and financial priorities, then make a shorter plan. The aim is meaningful preparation, not completing a particular number of days.

Ramadan 2027 at a Glance

  • Expected start date: Monday, February 8, 2027, or Tuesday, February 9, depending on the country and moon-sighting method.
  • Islamic year: Ramadan 1448 AH.
  • First Taraweeh prayers: Expected on the evening before the first fast.
  • Expected end of Ramadan: March 8 or March 9, depending on the confirmed start date and whether Ramadan lasts 29 or 30 days.
  • Expected Eid al-Fitr: Tuesday, March 9, or Wednesday, March 10, 2027.
  • Why dates differ: Countries and Muslim communities may follow local moon sightings, regional sightings, or pre-calculated Islamic calendars.
  • Important reminder: These are predictions, not final religious announcements. Check your local Islamic authority for confirmed dates.

When Does Ramadan 2027 Start?

Ramadan 2027 is expected to begin in February, bringing the holy month of fasting, prayer, Quran recitation, charity, and spiritual reflection to Muslims around the world.

According to commonly used Islamic calendars, the first day of Ramadan 1448 AH is expected to fall on Monday, February 8, 2027. However, communities that rely on local crescent-moon sightings may begin fasting on Tuesday, February 9 instead.

The exact date depends on the method used to determine the beginning of the Islamic month and the official announcement made by the relevant religious authority.

Expected Ramadan 2027 Dates

These dates are provisional. Communities may observe a different date depending on their calendar and moon-sighting decisions. Sources: Wego, Gulf News

Remember that the Islamic day begins at sunset. Therefore, if Ramadan begins on Monday, February 8, the first Taraweeh prayers are generally expected after sunset on Sunday, February 7.

Ramadan 2027 Dates in Bangladesh, Saudi Arabia, the UK and the USA

Ramadan does not necessarily begin on the same Gregorian date in every country. Differences in moon-sighting practices, geographical visibility, and calendar calculations can result in a one-day variation.

Here are the current expected dates for several countries and regions.

These are planning estimates, not guaranteed national announcements. Some organizations publish calculated dates in advance, while others wait for the relevant moon-sighting report. In Bangladesh, for example, the National Moon Sighting Committee determines the official dates. Sources: Wego, Niyat

If you live in a country where multiple Islamic organizations follow different methods, your local mosque may announce a date that differs from another community’s announcement.

The best approach is to follow the recognized Islamic authority or mosque that your community normally relies on.

Why Does Ramadan Start on Different Dates in Different Countries?

The Islamic calendar is based on the lunar cycle rather than the solar year used by the Gregorian calendar.

Each Islamic month begins with the new lunar month, which is traditionally established through crescent-moon sighting. Because the moon’s visibility depends on several factors, determining the beginning of Ramadan can involve both astronomical information and religious guidance.

There are three important reasons why dates may differ.

1. Local Moon Sighting

Some countries and communities require the crescent moon to be sighted locally or within a designated geographical region.

If the crescent cannot be confirmed on the expected evening, the preceding Islamic month may be completed as 30 days. Ramadan then begins the following day.

This approach follows the traditional practice of establishing the new month through crescent-moon observation.

2. Regional or Global Moon Sighting

Other communities accept a confirmed sighting from a wider geographical area or follow an established regional authority.

For example, one community may accept a verified sighting from another country, while another may require evidence from within its own region.

Consequently, two communities can make different decisions even when they have access to similar astronomical information.

3. Astronomical Calculations

Some Islamic organizations use astronomical calculations to determine dates in advance.

These calculations can estimate when the new moon occurs, when the moon sets relative to the sun, and whether the young crescent is likely to be visible.

However, the astronomical new moon and the first visible crescent are not the same thing. A new moon may occur before the crescent becomes visible after sunset.

Different calendar authorities also apply different criteria when deciding whether a month has begun. This is one reason calculated dates can differ from dates established through physical sighting.

How Does Moon Sighting Work?

Moon sighting is one of the most important traditions associated with the beginning and end of Ramadan.

After the 29th day of Sha’ban, the month before Ramadan, observers look for the thin crescent shortly after sunset.

The process generally involves the following steps:

  1. The expected observation evening arrives. Astronomers and moon-sighting committees identify when and where the crescent may be visible.
  2. Observers look toward the western horizon. The young crescent is usually sought shortly after sunset, weather and visibility permitting.
  3. Reports are collected. Depending on local procedures, witnesses may submit their observations to an authorized committee.
  4. The relevant authority evaluates the reports. The authority applies its established religious and astronomical criteria.
  5. The official announcement is made. Muslims are informed whether the next day will be the first of Ramadan or whether Sha’ban will be completed as 30 days.

Cloud cover, atmospheric conditions, the moon’s position, and the interval between sunset and moonset can affect visibility.

Modern technology can help astronomers predict visibility, but different religious authorities may still follow different procedures for accepting sightings.

For this reason, Ramadan dates published months in advance should always be treated as estimates when the final date depends on an official sighting.

When Is Eid al-Fitr 2027?

Eid al-Fitr, the festival marking the end of Ramadan, is expected to fall on Tuesday, March 9, or Wednesday, March 10, 2027.

The exact date depends on the beginning of Ramadan and the sighting of the crescent of Shawwal, the Islamic month that follows Ramadan.

If Ramadan begins on February 8 and lasts 29 days, Eid is expected on March 9. If the relevant calendar or moon-sighting decision places Eid one day later, it may fall on March 10.

Eid al-Fitr begins the Islamic month of Shawwal and is celebrated with the special Eid prayer, family gatherings, charity, and festive meals.

Muslims also give Zakat al-Fitr, a prescribed charity intended to help eligible people in need participate in the celebration. Its amount, timing, and practical requirements should be checked with a trusted local Islamic authority.

Because Eid dates are tied to the lunar calendar, anyone arranging travel, school holidays, family gatherings, or workplace leave should keep some flexibility in their plans.

How Long Will Ramadan 2027 Last?

Ramadan lasts either 29 or 30 days.

The length depends on the establishment of the next Islamic month, Shawwal. If the Shawwal crescent is confirmed according to the applicable rules after the 29th day of Ramadan, the month ends after 29 days. Otherwise, Ramadan completes 30 days.

For Ramadan 2027, the expected final fasting day is around March 8 or March 9, with Eid al-Fitr expected around March 9 or March 10.

A calendar published in advance may show a 29-day month, but communities that rely on moon sighting must wait for the relevant announcement before confirming the end date.

How to Prepare for Ramadan 2027

Although Ramadan 2027 is expected to begin in February, preparing early can help you approach the month with greater focus and consistency.

Here are five practical steps.

1. Prepare Your Worship Routine

Set realistic goals for Salah, Quran recitation, dua, and other acts of worship. Choose a routine that fits your responsibilities and that you can maintain throughout the month.

2. Adjust Your Sleep Schedule

Gradually prepare for waking up before dawn for suhoor and Fajr. Planning your sleep in advance can make the transition easier.

3. Plan Your Meals

Prepare balanced meal options for suhoor and iftar. Include nutritious foods, drink water regularly between sunset and dawn, and avoid making every iftar an excessively heavy meal.

4. Organize Your Responsibilities

If possible, complete important tasks before Ramadan and make a flexible schedule for work, studies, family commitments, and worship.

5. Set Spiritual Goals

Think about what you want to improve during Ramadan. You might focus on understanding the Quran, becoming more consistent with prayer, giving charity, or improving your character.

The purpose is not to create an impossible checklist. It is to make meaningful progress through sincere and consistent effort.

Frequently Asked Questions About Ramadan 2027

1. What is the exact date of Ramadan 2027?

The first fast is expected on Monday, February 8, 2027, in many calculated calendars. Some communities, including those that depend on local moon sighting, may begin on Tuesday, February 9. The final date will depend on the relevant announcement.

2. When is the first Taraweeh prayer in 2027?

If the first fast is Monday, February 8, the first Taraweeh prayers are expected after sunset on Sunday, February 7. If the first fast is Tuesday, February 9, Taraweeh would generally begin after sunset on Monday, February 8.

3. When is Eid al-Fitr 2027?

Eid al-Fitr is expected on Tuesday, March 9, or Wednesday, March 10, 2027. The confirmed date depends on the calendar or moon-sighting method followed by your community.

4. Will Ramadan 2027 begin on the same day worldwide?

Not necessarily. Differences in geographical moon visibility, local and regional sighting policies, and calculated calendars can lead to a one-day difference between communities.

5. Why can Ramadan dates change at the last minute?

A predicted date may change because the crescent is not confirmed according to the relevant authority’s criteria. If the preceding Islamic month reaches 30 days, Ramadan begins the following day.

6. Will Ramadan 2027 last 29 or 30 days?

It may last either 29 or 30 days. The end of Ramadan is established according to the beginning of Shawwal, using the relevant moon-sighting or calendar method.

7. Is Ramadan 2027 in February or March?

Ramadan 2027 is expected to begin in February and continue into March. Eid al-Fitr is expected in March.

8. How can I find Ramadan 2027 Sehri and Iftar times?

The Complete Ramadan Guide for Beginners

Long Story Short…

Ramadan is the ninth month of the Islamic calendar and one of the holiest times of the year for Muslims. During this month, Muslims fast from dawn until sunset, abstaining from food, drink, and other things that break the fast. But Ramadan is about much more than going hungry. It is a time to strengthen your relationship with Allah, practice self-discipline, seek forgiveness, give to those in need, and develop better habits. Whether you are experiencing Ramadan for the first time or looking to make the most of it, this guide covers everything you need to know, from the meaning of fasting to spiritual preparation, healthy eating, daily worship, and making Ramadan more meaningful.

What Is Ramadan?

Ramadan is the ninth month of the Islamic lunar calendar and a sacred month for Muslims around the world. It is a time of fasting, prayer, reflection, charity, and spiritual growth.

Ramadan holds a special place in Islam because it was during this month that the Quran began to be revealed to Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). The Quran describes Ramadan as the month in which the guidance for humanity was revealed.

For Muslims, Ramadan offers an opportunity to pause from the distractions of everyday life and focus on what matters most: faith, gratitude, good character, and closeness to Allah.

The month lasts either 29 or 30 days, depending on the sighting of the new crescent moon. Since the Islamic calendar follows the lunar cycle, Ramadan moves approximately 10 to 11 days earlier each year in the Gregorian calendar.

Across the world, Ramadan brings communities together. Families share meals before dawn and after sunset, mosques welcome worshippers for additional prayers, and people increase their acts of kindness and generosity.

However, the heart of Ramadan is not simply its traditions. It is the opportunity to become a better Muslim, one day at a time.

Why Do Muslims Fast During Ramadan?

Fasting during Ramadan is one of the Five Pillars of Islam, making it a fundamental act of worship for eligible Muslims.

In the Quran, Allah says:

“O you who have believed, decreed upon you is fasting as it was decreed upon those before you that you may become righteous.”

Surah Al-Baqarah 2:183

This verse explains the deeper purpose of fasting: developing taqwa, which means God-consciousness. It is the awareness that Allah sees us, knows our intentions, and deserves our sincere obedience.

1. To Strengthen the Relationship With Allah

Fasting is an act of worship performed for Allah. Even when nobody else is watching, a fasting person chooses to abstain from food and drink out of faith and obedience.

This private act of devotion can strengthen sincerity and encourage Muslims to become more mindful of their Creator throughout the day.

2. To Develop Self-Discipline

Ramadan teaches Muslims to control their desires and make conscious choices.

Hunger, thirst, frustration, and temptation can become opportunities to practice patience. Instead of reacting with anger, a person can learn to respond calmly. Instead of following every desire, they can practice restraint.

These lessons can extend far beyond Ramadan.

3. To Appreciate What We Have

It is easy to overlook everyday blessings when they are always available. Fasting reminds Muslims that food, clean water, health, and comfort are gifts worth appreciating.

Experiencing hunger can also encourage empathy for people who face food insecurity and other hardships every day.

4. To Seek Forgiveness and Renew Faith

Ramadan is an opportunity to turn back to Allah, sincerely repent for past mistakes, and renew one’s commitment to living according to Islamic teachings.

Muslims seek forgiveness, make dua, increase their prayers, and try to leave harmful habits behind.

5. To Become More Compassionate

Charity and kindness are especially emphasized during Ramadan. Muslims are encouraged to feed people in need, support struggling families, give Zakat and voluntary charity, and treat others with generosity.

The goal is not merely to experience hardship but to let that experience inspire compassion and meaningful action.

Who Is Required to Fast?

Fasting during Ramadan is obligatory for adult Muslims who are physically and mentally capable of fasting and meet the relevant Islamic conditions.

Islam recognizes that people face different circumstances. Certain individuals may be exempt from fasting or permitted to postpone it.

These include:

  • Children who have not reached puberty.
  • People who are ill and for whom fasting would cause harm.
  • Travelers who qualify for the Islamic travel concession.
  • Pregnant or breastfeeding women when fasting may cause harm to them or their child, subject to the applicable Islamic rulings.
  • Women who are menstruating or experiencing postnatal bleeding.
  • Older people and individuals with conditions that make fasting permanently unsafe, who may have different obligations under Islamic law.

The requirements for making up missed fasts or providing compensation vary according to the circumstances and scholarly rulings. Anyone unsure about their situation should consult a knowledgeable Islamic scholar. People with medical conditions should also seek appropriate medical advice.

Islam emphasizes both devotion and mercy. Fasting should be approached with an understanding of the concessions Allah has provided.

How Does Fasting Work During Ramadan?

A Ramadan fast begins at dawn and ends at sunset.

Suhoor: The Pre-Dawn Meal

Suhoor is the meal eaten before dawn, before the fasting period begins. It provides nourishment and hydration for the day ahead.

Although people sometimes skip suhoor because they feel sleepy or are not hungry, having a balanced meal can make fasting more manageable.

Good options include oats, eggs, whole-grain bread, yogurt, fruit, vegetables, and other nutritious foods. Drinking enough water before dawn is also important.

Avoid relying heavily on salty, very sugary, or highly processed foods, as these may make the day less comfortable.

Fasting Throughout the Day

From dawn until sunset, fasting Muslims abstain from food, drinks, and other actions that invalidate the fast according to Islamic teachings.

Muslims also make an effort to avoid gossip, lying, backbiting, arguments, and harmful behavior.

A fast is not only about controlling physical needs. It is also about guarding the tongue, managing anger, and protecting the heart from negativity.

Iftar: Breaking the Fast

Iftar is the meal eaten at sunset to break the fast.

Many Muslims follow the tradition of breaking their fast with dates and water, then performing the Maghrib prayer before continuing their meal.

Iftar is often shared with family, friends, neighbors, and people in need. It can be a joyful time of gratitude and community.

For a healthier iftar, start with water and a moderate portion of food. Include vegetables, protein, whole grains, and other nourishing foods rather than eating too much fried or sugary food at once.

Taraweeh: The Special Night Prayers

Taraweeh refers to additional prayers performed at night during Ramadan, usually after the Isha prayer.

Many Muslims attend the mosque for Taraweeh, while others pray at home. The prayers often include recitation of the Quran.

Taraweeh is a recommended act of worship, not a condition for a valid fast. Beginners can start with a manageable routine and gradually increase their participation.

How to Prepare Spiritually for Ramadan

A meaningful Ramadan begins with intention, not perfection. You do not need to transform your entire life overnight. Start with a few sincere steps and build consistency.

1. Renew Your Intention

Ask yourself what you want to gain from Ramadan.

Perhaps you want to become more consistent with Salah, reconnect with the Quran, overcome a bad habit, improve your character, or feel closer to Allah.

Write down two or three personal goals and revisit them throughout the month.

2. Build a Quran Routine

You do not have to read large portions of the Quran immediately to begin benefiting from it.

Start with a realistic daily target. Read a few pages, study the meaning of a short surah, or listen to a recitation while following the translation.

Understanding even a small portion of the Quran can help make your worship more thoughtful and personal.

Consistency matters more than setting a goal that becomes difficult to maintain.

3. Become More Consistent With Salah

Use the days before Ramadan to establish a regular prayer routine if you have struggled with consistency.

Learn the prayer times in your area, prepare a clean prayer space, and organize your schedule around Salah rather than fitting prayer into whatever time remains.

During Ramadan, aim to protect all five obligatory prayers and gradually improve your focus and understanding.

4. Make Dua Every Day

Dua is a personal conversation with Allah. Ask for forgiveness, guidance, patience, good health, and the strength to become a better Muslim.

You can make dua in Arabic or in your own language. Speak honestly about your struggles, hopes, and intentions.

Consider keeping a small list of duas you want to remember throughout Ramadan.

5. Plan Your Charity

Charity does not have to be limited to large financial contributions.

You can feed someone, support a family in need, help a neighbor, donate to a trustworthy cause, or offer your time and skills.

If Zakat is due on your wealth, learn how to calculate and distribute it correctly. Zakat is an obligatory form of charity with specific rules, while Sadaqah is voluntary.

6. Leave Room for Repentance and Growth

You may enter Ramadan with habits you are unhappy with or mistakes you wish you could undo.

Do not let shame prevent you from trying again.

Make sincere repentance, take practical steps to avoid repeating harmful behavior, and remember that spiritual growth is a process.

The purpose of Ramadan is not to appear perfect. It is to seek Allah’s guidance and keep returning to Him.

How to Prepare Physically for Ramadan

Spiritual preparation matters, but taking care of your body can also help you worship more comfortably.

Adjust your sleep schedule. Start moving your bedtime earlier if you expect to wake up for suhoor. If possible, create time for rest during the day.

Stay hydrated. Drink water regularly between iftar and suhoor instead of trying to drink a large amount all at once. Individual hydration needs vary.

Choose balanced meals. Include protein, fiber-rich carbohydrates, vegetables, fruit, and healthy fats. These can support energy and help you feel satisfied for longer.

Avoid overeating. Eating excessively at iftar may leave you feeling uncomfortable and make nighttime worship more difficult.

Maintain gentle physical activity. Walking or light exercise can help you stay active. Adjust intensity according to your energy levels and personal health needs.

Manage existing health conditions. If you take regular medication or have a medical condition, consult your healthcare professional before Ramadan to discuss whether fasting is safe and whether your treatment schedule needs adjustment.

Seek medical advice if you experience concerning symptoms during fasting. Protecting your health is important, and Islamic concessions exist for people who cannot safely fast.

The Last Ten Nights of Ramadan

The final ten nights of Ramadan hold particular spiritual significance.

Among these nights is Laylatul Qadr, the Night of Decree, which the Quran describes as better than a thousand months.

Muslims seek this blessed night during the last ten nights, especially the odd-numbered nights, following the teachings of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him).

During this period, many Muslims increase their prayers, Quran recitation, dua, repentance, and charity.

You can prepare by reducing unnecessary distractions, organizing your responsibilities in advance, and making time for worship.

Even if you cannot spend entire nights in prayer, sincere and consistent acts of worship are valuable. Focus on what you can realistically maintain.

Common Mistakes Beginners Should Avoid

Treating Ramadan as only a food restriction. Hunger and thirst are part of fasting, but the deeper goal is spiritual growth and better character.

Trying to do everything at once. Setting too many ambitious goals can lead to exhaustion. Start with a few priorities and build from there.

Neglecting sleep and health. Constant exhaustion can make worship and daily responsibilities harder. Plan your rest as carefully as your worship.

Overeating at iftar. Large, heavy meals can leave you uncomfortable and reduce your energy.

Becoming discouraged after a difficult day. Some days will be easier than others. If you fall short of a personal goal, return to it the next day instead of giving up.

Focusing only on yourself. Ramadan is also a time to strengthen family relationships, forgive others when appropriate, help your community, and practice kindness.

A Simple Daily Ramadan Routine for Beginners

You can adapt the following routine to your local prayer times, work schedule, and energy levels.

  • Before dawn: Wake up for suhoor, drink water, make your intention, and pray Fajr.
  • Morning: Begin your daily responsibilities and spend a few minutes reading the Quran.
  • Afternoon: Continue your work or studies, protect your prayers, and avoid unnecessary arguments or distractions.
  • Before iftar: Make dua, prepare to break your fast, and help others where possible.
  • At sunset: Break your fast, pray Maghrib, and eat a balanced meal.
  • Evening: Pray Isha and Taraweeh if possible, spend time with family, and prepare for the next day.
  • Before sleeping: Reflect on your day, seek forgiveness, and make a simple plan for tomorrow.

Remember that this is a flexible guide, not a checklist you must complete perfectly every day.

Make This Ramadan Your Starting Point

Ramadan is a chance to reset your priorities, strengthen your faith, and build habits that continue long after the month ends.

You do not need to begin with perfect knowledge or an elaborate worship routine. Start with sincere intentions, learn what you can, take small steps, and remain consistent.

Protect your prayers. Make time for the Quran. Be mindful of your words. Give generously. Take care of your health. And when you make a mistake, return to Allah with hope.

The real success of Ramadan is not simply reaching Eid after thirty days of fasting. It is carrying the lessons of Ramadan into the rest of your life.

Make Your Ramadan More Meaningful With Muslims Day

Assalamu ‘alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

The Ansar of Madinah did not lead the caravan. They opened their homes to it. Because of them, a message survived, spread, and reached across the world. Every person who has ever given, in any amount, to keep the Muslims Day app running stands in that same tradition today. You do not appear on any screen in this app. No user will ever know your name. And yet nothing you are about to read would have happened without you.

This is an account of what your support made possible over the past 31 days – and a reminder of why quiet, sustained giving matters more than most of us realize.

What You Made Possible

In just 31 days, Muslims Day carried the call to prayer 61 million times to 1.1 million Muslims around the world.

Sit with that number for a moment. Sixty-one million reminders work out to roughly 2.18 million every single day – about fifty-five for every person who uses the app. Somewhere in Dhaka, in Riyadh, in Paris, a phone buzzed at Fajr, and someone got up who might otherwise have slept through it. Multiply that moment by 61 million, and you start to see the shape of what quiet generosity actually builds.

Here is the fuller picture of what happened in a single month:

Taken together, the people this community serves spent more than 480,000 hours inside this app in a single month. That is over 20,000 days – more than fifty-four years of human time, lived inside one month, spent turning toward prayer, Qur’an, and du’a. Fifty-four years of attention pointed toward Allah, made possible by people most users will never meet and never thank by name.

“So establish the prayer. Indeed, the prayer has been appointed at fixed times.” (Meaning of Surah an-Nisa’ 4:103)

Acts of Prayer, Not Statistics

It is easy for numbers like these to blur together into an abstraction. So here is what those numbers actually were, broken down over the past 28 days:

Behind each row is a person, not a data point. The 153,000 who read Qur’an inside the app opened it 1.4 million times – roughly nine sittings each. For many of them, this app is the only Qur’an they carry with them, tucked into a pocket between shifts, between train stops, between the ordinary demands of a day that leaves little room for anything else.

The 126,000 who reached for du’a did so 2.8 million times – about twenty-two times each. These are not casual taps. These are people looking for the right words at a hard moment, and finding them, at 2am or in a hospital waiting room or on a walk they needed to take alone.

And 186,000 people deliberately set an alarm for prayer. That is not a passive download sitting unused on a home screen. That is a decision, made again and again, to be woken.

“Whoever guides another to something good receives a reward like the one who acts upon it.” (Meaning of a hadith reported in Sahih Muslim)

Sixty-one million reminders were sixty-one million small acts of guidance toward something good. What is written for the people who made those reminders possible is with Allah alone – but the hope contained in that is not small.

Where the Ummah Was Reached

Bangladesh remains the heart of this work. Over the past 28 days:

But the app has travelled far beyond home. In a single recent week it was used across India, Indonesia, Saudi Arabia, France, Germany, and Brazil.

Think about who those people actually are. A construction worker in the Gulf, far from his family, with no masjid within hearing distance. A student in Germany who has no idea when Maghrib falls in a city that isn’t hers. A Bangladeshi driver in Riyadh with nobody around to remind him. For every one of them, the adhan now comes from a pocket – because a community of contributors, most of whom will never meet these people, paid quietly for it to be there.

Not a Download. A Daily Habit.

It is easy to install an app and forget it exists a week later. That is not what is happening here.

More than one in three monthly users opens Muslims Day on any given day. Very few apps in the world come close to that kind of return rate. It means this has stopped being software people happened to install and has become part of the actual rhythm of people’s prayer – which is precisely what a tool built for prayer should be.

At the exact moment this report was compiled, around 7,900 Muslims were using the app in that same instant. Nearly seven thousands of them were in Bangladesh.

There was one day in particular worth remembering: on 21 July 2026, 959,014 people used Muslims Day in a single day – more than the app’s own forecasting systems believed was statistically possible. The system flagged it as an anomaly. It is easier, and truer, to read it as a mercy. Around that same week, usage across Bangladesh rose by 119% compared to the week before.

Free for Every Muslim, and Staying That Way

Out of 1.1 million people served this month, almost none of them were ever asked for anything.

There is no paywall on prayer times. No subscription fee for the Qur’an. No charge to be reminded of Fajr. A rickshaw puller in Gazipur and a professional working in Dhaka open the exact same app, with the exact same access, side by side.

That is only possible because a small number of people quietly carry the cost for everybody else. That is what all of our contributors do, every single month, without recognition and without asking for any.

The Road Ahead

There is still real work in front of this project, and it’s worth being transparent about what that looks like.

iPhone users are still barely served. Almost everyone reached today is on Android, which means many brothers and sisters overseas – especially across the Gulf and Europe, where iPhone usage skews much higher – are not yet properly reached at all. Bringing the app to full strength on iPhone is the next major undertaking.

More languages, more places. France, Germany, Brazil, Indonesia, and India are already among the countries using the app organically, without any dedicated outreach. Proper translation and locally accurate prayer times would open the door far wider for comparatively little additional cost.

A faster, simpler app. Older screens are being consolidated so that every user – including those on slow connections and older, budget phones – gets the same clean, reliable experience regardless of where they live or what device they can afford.

Continued support from all of our contributors is what turns each of these from a stated intention into a released update that actually reaches someone at Fajr tomorrow.

A Word of Thanks

“Three things continue after a person is gone: an ongoing charity, knowledge of benefit, and a righteous child who prays for them.” (Meaning of a hadith reported in Sahih Muslim)

This app is running right now, in this exact minute, while you read this. It will ring at Fajr tomorrow in cities none of our contributors will ever visit, for people they will never meet, in languages they may not even speak. Sadaqah jariyah is not an abstract metaphor here – it is the literal, ongoing shape of what has been built, one contribution at a time.

All of our contributors are the Ansar of this work – the ones who opened the door and made room, without ever needing to be seen doing it. Thank you for standing where you stand.

Jazakum Allahu khayran. May Allah accept it from you, multiply it for you, place it in your scales on the Day when scales are all that matter, and make you among those who are pleased with Him and with whom He is pleased.

item.content:encoded:
Plants Are a Blessing from Allah

Plants, trees, and all forms of vegetation are among the countless blessings of Allah Almighty. They are indispensable for maintaining the balance and harmony of the earth. Whether humans or animals, the primary source of food for all living beings comes from plants; they make the earth lush and green. Trees help reduce the planet’s rising temperature. Weary travelers find cool shade beneath them. Their branches and dry leaves serve as firewood. Large trees are cut into timber and transformed into beautiful furniture. The leaves of some trees, the fruits of others, and even the bark of certain trees are used as medicine or as raw materials for producing medicine. And these are only a few of the countless benefits of trees, plants, and vines.


This Blessing Mentioned in the Holy Qur’an

The Holy Qur’an repeatedly draws our attention to this great blessing bestowed by Allah. Consider a few examples:

فَلْیَنْظُرِ الْاِنْسَانُ اِلٰى طَعَامِهٖۤۙ ۝۲۴ اَنَّا صَبَبْنَا الْمَآءَ صَبًّاۙ ۝۲۵ ثُمَّ شَقَقْنَا الْاَرْضَ شَقًّاۙ ۝۲۶ فَاَنْۢبَتْنَا فِیْهَا حَبًّاۙ ۝۲۷ وَّ عِنَبًا وَّ قَضْبًاۙ ۝۲۸ وَّ زَیْتُوْنًا وَّ نَخْلًاۙ ۝۲۹ وَّ حَدَآىِٕقَ غُلْبًاۙ ۝۳۰ وَّ فَاكِهَةً وَّ اَبًّاۙ ۝۳۱ مَّتَاعًا لَّكُمْ وَ لِاَنْعَامِكُمْؕ ۝۳۲

Translation: “Let man then look at his food. Indeed, We poured down water in abundance. Then We split the earth open, causing grain to grow from it, along with grapes, vegetables, olives, date palms, dense gardens, fruits, and grass, as a provision for you and for your livestock.”

(Surah ‘Abasa, Verses 24–32)

These verses mention a remarkable variety of plants. They speak of towering trees such as date palms, climbing vines like grapes, different kinds of grains and vegetables, and even the grass that appears to grow on its own without human care.

For all these plants to grow, and even for a tiny seed to sprout, Allah Almighty sends rain down from the heavens. With just a touch of rainwater, hard earth splits apart, allowing tender green shoots to emerge. Is this alone not sufficient evidence of Allah’s infinite power?

In these verses, Allah directs human beings to reflect upon their food. Where does this endless variety of nourishment come from? By whose command do plants grow? Who creates the conditions that allow grass, trees, and crops to flourish?

Although these blessings surround us every day, each one is a profound sign of Allah’s limitless power and mercy. The Holy Qur’an presents another remarkable example:

وَ اٰیَةٌ لَّهُمُ الْاَرْضُ الْمَیْتَةُ ۖ ۚ اَحْیَیْنٰهَا وَ اَخْرَجْنَا مِنْهَا حَبًّا فَمِنْهُ یَاْكُلُوْنَ ۝۳۳ وَ جَعَلْنَا فِیْهَا جَنّٰتٍ مِّنْ نَّخِیْلٍ وَّ اَعْنَابٍ وَّ فَجَّرْنَا فِیْهَا مِنَ الْعُیُوْنِۙ ۝۳۴ لِیَاْكُلُوْا مِنْ ثَمَرِهٖ ۙ وَ مَا عَمِلَتْهُ اَیْدِیْهِمْ ؕ اَفَلَا یَشْكُرُوْنَ ۝۳۵ سُبْحٰنَ الَّذِیْ خَلَقَ الْاَزْوَاجَ كُلَّهَا مِمَّا تُنْۢبِتُ الْاَرْضُ وَ مِنْ اَنْفُسِهِمْ وَ مِمَّا لَا یَعْلَمُوْنَ ۝۳۶

Translation: A sign for them is the dead earth. We give it life and bring forth from it grain, from which they eat. We have placed therein gardens of date palms and grapevines, and caused springs to gush forth, so that they may eat from their fruits. Yet it was not their hands that produced them. Will they not then give thanks? Glory be to the One Who created all things in pairs: what the earth produces, what they themselves are, and even what they do not yet know.

(Surah Ya-Sin, Verses 33–36)

The words, “Yet it was not their hands that produced them. Will they not then give thanks?”, deserve special attention. In these verses, Allah Almighty makes it abundantly clear that barren and lifeless land is revived by the rain He sends down from the heavens. The hardened earth splits apart, tender shoots emerge from within, and in time those shoots become fields of grain, flourishing grapevines, or towering date palms. Eventually, people harvest their fruits and consume them as their sustenance. Yet this provision is not the creation of human hands.

A person may plant a small sapling or sow a seed in the soil, but that is the extent of human ability. Does anyone possess the power to nurture that seed into a flourishing tree adorned with flowers and laden with fruit? Certainly not. It is Allah Almighty alone Who brings about its growth. This is exactly what He makes clear in these verses: the provisions we enjoy are not the work of our own hands. They are blessings from Allah, manifestations of His infinite mercy and His perfect creation.

Grafted saplings can be planted throughout the year. However, the ideal season for tree plantation is during the months of June, July, and August. Let us plant improved varieties of saplings and contribute to a greener, healthier world.

The Holy Qur’an makes this reality even clearer in another verse:

اَفَرَءَیْتُمْ مَّا تَحْرُثُوْنَؕ ۝۶۳ ءَاَنْتُمْ تَزْرَعُوْنَهٗۤ اَمْ نَحْنُ الزّٰرِعُوْنَ ۝۶۴

Translation: “Have you considered what you sow? Is it you who make it grow, or are We the One Who causes it to grow?”

(Surah Al-Waqi’ah, Verses 63–64)

In other words, do we truly possess the power to make the seeds we sow split open and sprout into living plants? All we can do is place a seed into the soil with our own hands. Nothing more. At most, we can transplant a young sapling from one place to another. Beyond that, we have no power whatsoever. We cannot command a seed to germinate, breathe life into it, or make it grow. That extraordinary process belongs to Allah alone.

Tree Plantation in the Light of the Hadith

Allah Almighty nurtures the seeds we sow and the saplings we plant, allowing them to grow into flourishing trees adorned with flowers and fruit. From them, we receive our sustenance. By itself, this is already an immense blessing. Yet the mercy of Allah does not end there. Through these trees, He provides us with food, helps maintain the balance of our environment, offers us cool shade, and grants us countless other benefits. These are rewards we enjoy in this world. Beyond all of these, however, Allah has also reserved everlasting rewards in the Hereafter for those who plant trees. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

مَا مِنْ مُسْلِمٍ يَغْرِسُ غَرْسًا ، أَوْ يَزْرَعُ زَرْعًا فَيَأْكُلُ مِنْهُ طَيْرٌ ، أَوْ إِنْسَانٌ ، أَوْ بَهِيمَةٌ إِلاَّ كَانَ لَهُ بِهِ صَدَقَةٌ

Translation: “Whenever a Muslim plants a tree or cultivates a crop, and a bird, a person, or an animal eats from it, it is counted as an act of charity (Sadaqah) for him.”

(Sahih al-Bukhari, Hadith 2320)

Tree Plantation in Islam is not merely an act of cultivating the earth; it is an act of worship that continues to benefit both the planter and others. People usually plant trees to enjoy their fruits themselves or to provide for their families in the future. Naturally, one expects to eat the fruit of a tree that one has planted with one’s own hands. There is nothing unusual about that. Yet the beauty of this teaching is that even when the planter himself enjoys its fruits, or when any other person benefits from them, every such benefit is recorded by Allah as an act of charity on behalf of the one who planted the tree.

Human beings are the noblest of Allah’s creation. Yet even if a grazing animal eats from that tree, or a bird pecks at its fruit, reducing what the owner might have harvested, the planter does not lose his reward. Instead, Allah records it as an act of charity for him.

Even more remarkable is another narration of the Prophet ﷺ. He taught that if someone steals the fruit from a tree, the owner and the one who planted it are still rewarded. The Hadith states:

مَا مِنْ مُسْلِمٍ يَغْرِسُ غَرْسًا إِلاَّ كَانَ مَا أُكِلَ مِنْهُ لَهُ صَدَقَةٌ وَمَا سُرِقَ مِنْهُ لَهُ صَدَقَةٌ وَمَا أَكَلَ السَّبُعُ مِنْهُ فَهُوَ لَهُ صَدَقَةٌ وَمَا أَكَلَتِ الطَّيْرُ فَهُوَ لَهُ صَدَقَةً وَلاَ يَرْزَؤُهُ أَحَدٌ إِلاَّ كَانَ لَهُ صَدَقَةٌ

Translation: “Whenever a Muslim plants a tree, whatever is eaten from it is counted as charity for him; whatever is stolen from it is counted as charity for him; whatever is eaten by wild animals is counted as charity for him; whatever is eaten by birds is counted as charity for him; and whatever anyone takes from it is also counted as charity for him.”

(Sahih Muslim, Hadith 1552)

Just imagine how many different ways a single tree can become a source of Sadaqah. Feeding another person earns reward. Eating from its fruits yourself also earns reward. Even if someone steals its fruits without permission, or birds and animals consume them before you do, Allah still records every one of those losses as charity in your account.

What is even more extraordinary is that this reward is not limited to a person’s lifetime. If someone plants a tree and then passes away, as long as that tree continues to bear fruit and benefit Allah’s creation, its planter continues to receive reward. In this sense, planting a tree becomes a form of Sadaqah Jariyah—a continuous charity whose rewards endure long after one’s life has come to an end.

Tree Plantation Is an Act of Service

Tree Plantation in Islam is not limited to planting fruit-bearing trees for the reward of Sadaqah. Besides this, there are many other ways in which planting trees earns reward. If someone plants a shade tree beside a road, and it eventually grows large enough to provide cool shade for travelers, he will also be rewarded. Providing comfort to weary travelers through its shade is itself a source of reward.

Tree Plantation in Islam also encourages believers to plant trees with the sincere intention of benefiting others. For example, by planting fruit trees, one may intend to feed people with their fruits. If it is another type of tree, it may later provide useful materials such as timber or firewood. Likewise, a farmer may cultivate crops as his profession and earn his livelihood by selling them, yet he may also intend to benefit others through his work. A believer is rewarded according to his intention.

Another important aspect of this intention is that trees are among the most effective means of reducing global warming. People throughout the world benefit from this. A single tree planted by one person may not reduce the temperature of the entire planet, but if tree planting becomes a movement across the world, it will certainly make a significant contribution to reducing global temperatures. Not only human beings, but animals and birds will also benefit from it. Undoubtedly, every creature belongs to the family of Allah. The Prophet ﷺ said:

الْخَلْقُ عِيَالُ اللهِ، وَأَحَبُّ الْعِبَادِ إِلَى اللهِ أَنْفَعُهُمْ لِعِيَالِهِ

Translation: “All creation is the family of Allah, and the most beloved of Allah’s servants are those who are most beneficial to His creation.”

(Shu’ab al-Iman, Hadith 7045)

Therefore, tree plantation can become a unique means of serving Allah’s creation. Let this social movement begin today. It may be difficult for one person, or even ten people, to plant ten million saplings. But it is not difficult for ten million people. So let us plant trees, serve Allah’s creation, and protect the environment.

item.title: 10 Must-Have Muslim Lifestyle Apps for New Muslims
item.description: Best muslim lifestyle apps suggestion for the new muslims who are in need ot daily guidance of islamic rules.
item.content:encoded:
Embracing Islam is a beautiful, life-changing journey – but for new Muslims (reverts), it can also feel overwhelming at first. Learning the prayers, memorizing duas, understanding the Quran, and building consistent habits all take time. Thankfully, technology has made this transition significantly easier. A good Muslim lifestyle app can act as a daily companion, guiding you through prayer times, Quran recitation, duas, and more – all from your phone.

In this listicle, we’re breaking down the must-have Muslim lifestyle apps every new Muslim should consider downloading, starting with the most beginner-friendly, all-in-one option.

Short Read..

New to Islam and not sure which apps to download? Here’s the shortlist:

  1. Muslims Day – Best all-in-one app for beginners (prayer times, Quran, duas, Qibla, Bangla + English support)
  2. Muslim Pro – Most popular global Muslim lifestyle app with Islamic content, community feed, and habit tracking
  3. IslamicFinder – Trusted source for accurate prayer times, Islamic calendar, and educational content
  4. The Pillars – Minimalist, privacy-focused app great for building consistent prayer habits
  5. Athan – Reliable, no-frills app focused on adhan notifications and Qibla direction
  6. Muslim Bangla – Comprehensive Bangla-language app, ideal for Bengali-speaking new Muslims
  7. Tarteel – AI-powered app for learning Quran recitation and memorization
  8. Zabihah -The go-to halal restaurant, market, and prayer-space finder
  9. Sunnah.com App – Authentic hadith collections for building Islamic knowledge
  10. Muslim & Quran – Prayer time app with prayer history logging and multilingual support

Read on for a detailed breakdown of each.

1. Muslims Day – Best All-in-One App for New Muslims

If you’re just starting your journey and want one app that covers everything without complexity, Muslims Day is the top pick. It’s designed with simplicity in mind, making it especially beginner-friendly for new Muslims who are still learning the basics of daily worship.

Key Features:

  • 🕌 Accurate prayer times for all five daily prayers (Fajr, Dhuhr, Asr, Maghrib, Isha), plus optional prayers like Duha, Tahajjud, and Ishrak
  • ⏱️ Prayer alarms, notifications, and a countdown timer for the current Salat window
  • 📖 Quran, Tafseer, and Hadith access
  • 📿 Daily duas and Asmaul Husna (99 Names of Allah)
  • 🧭 Built-in Qibla compass
  • 🌍 Available in both English and Bangla – ideal for Bengali-speaking new Muslims and their families
  • 🌙 Special seasonal content, such as Ramadan Sehri/Iftar timings and virtues of Dhul-Hijjah

Why It’s Great for New Muslims: As a new Muslim, having a single, uncluttered app that walks you through your five daily prayers – with reminders and simple explanations – removes a lot of the early guesswork. Muslims Day keeps everything essential in one place, without overwhelming you with unnecessary features.

[Download Muslims Day for iOS]

[Download Muslims Day for Android]

2. Muslim Pro – Most Popular Global Muslim Lifestyle App

Muslim Pro is one of the most widely downloaded Muslim lifestyle apps in the world, with a large global user base. It offers a comprehensive suite of features, making it a strong choice for new Muslims who want a feature-rich experience.

Key Features:

  • Accurate, location-based prayer times with customizable Athan (Adhan) alerts
  • Full Holy Quran with translations in 40+ languages, audio recitations, and memorization tools
  • Qibla compass and Islamic (Hijri) calendar
  • Daily duas and azkar, plus a digital Tasbih counter
  • Halal restaurant and mosque finder
  • Community feed to connect with other Muslims
  • Islamic educational content, including films and articles (via Qalbox)

Why It’s Great for New Muslims: The sheer breadth of content – from beginner-friendly Quran tools to a built-in community feed – makes Muslim Pro a solid choice for reverts who want to explore Islamic learning materials alongside their daily prayer routine. Note that some advanced features require a premium subscription.

3. IslamicFinder – Trusted Source for Prayer Times & Islamic Knowledge

IslamicFinder has long been recognized as one of the most trusted names for accurate prayer times and Islamic educational resources, both on the web and through its mobile apps.

Key Features:

  • Verified, location-based prayer times using multiple calculation methods
  • Qibla direction finder
  • Islamic calendar with important dates (Ramadan, Eid, etc.)
  • Access to Quran, Hadith, and dua collections
  • Zakat calculator and Islamic date converter
  • Regularly updated blog content covering Islamic knowledge and lifestyle topics

Why It’s Great for New Muslims: Beyond just prayer times, IslamicFinder’s strength lies in its educational content – making it a good companion app for new Muslims who want to deepen their understanding of Islamic practices alongside their daily worship routine.

5. The Pillars – Minimalist, Privacy-Focused Prayer App

For new Muslims who want a simple, distraction-free way to build the habit of praying five times a day, The Pillars is an excellent choice. Built by Muslims with a strong focus on privacy, this app strips away unnecessary clutter and focuses on the essentials.

Key Features:

  • Clean, minimalist prayer times and Qibla compass
  • Prayer tracker – specifically designed to help new converts and those building consistency in their salah
  • Fasting tracker to log missed fasts and mark makeup days
  • A “menstruation pause” feature so tracking streaks aren’t broken
  • Home screen and lock screen widgets for quick access
  • Strong privacy focus – location data stays on your device and isn’t sent to external servers

Why It’s Great for New Muslims: The built-in prayer tracker is particularly valuable for reverts, since it’s specifically designed to help you build the habit of praying consistently – one of the most important early steps in a new Muslim’s journey.

5. Athan – Reliable, No-Frills Prayer & Qibla App

Athan, developed by IslamicFinder, is a straightforward, no-frills app focused specifically on two core needs: prayer time notifications and Qibla direction.

Key Features:

  • Automatic Athan (call to prayer) playback at prayer times
  • Built-in compass for accurate Qibla direction
  • 12-hour and 24-hour time format options
  • Quran recitations
  • Simple, easy-to-navigate interface

Why It’s Great for New Muslims: If you’re looking for an app that does the basics extremely well without extra clutter, Athan is a dependable option. Its simplicity makes it especially approachable for someone who’s still getting used to the rhythm of daily prayers.

6. Muslim Bangla – Best for Bengali-Speaking New Muslims

For Bengali-speaking new Muslims, or those with family and community ties to Bangladesh, Muslim Bangla offers a comprehensive Islamic lifestyle experience fully localized in the Bangla language.

Key Features:

  • Prayer times and Adhan alerts in Bangla and English
  • Full Quran with Bangla translation and recitation
  • Hadith collections (Sahih Bukhari, Sahih Muslim, and more)
  • Daily dua and Zakat/Sadaka tools
  • “Ask Scholars” Q&A feature and voice call access to a Mufti for direct guidance
  • Qibla compass, mosque finder, and Hajj/Umrah guide
  • Islamic calendar, 99 Names of Allah, and live Makkah streaming

Why It’s Great for New Muslims: Language matters a lot in the early stages of learning Islam. For Bengali speakers, having prayer instructions, Quran translations, and scholarly guidance available in their native language makes the learning curve significantly smoother.

7. Tarteel – AI-Powered Quran Recitation & Memorization

For new Muslims eager to learn to read and eventually memorize the Quran, Tarteel is one of the most innovative tools available. It uses AI-powered voice recognition to listen to your recitation and give real-time feedback.

Key Features:

  • Voice-recognition technology that listens as you recite and highlights mistakes in real time
  • “Shazam for Quran” – recite any phrase and the app instantly finds the matching Ayah and Surah
  • Mistake history tracking to help you focus on recurring errors
  • Multiple Qira’at (recitation styles) and reciter options
  • Hidden verse/peeking mode to test memorization progress
  • Translations and tafsir available alongside the Arabic text

Why It’s Great for New Muslims: Learning to read Arabic script and recite the Quran correctly can feel intimidating at first. Tarteel acts like a patient, always-available practice partner – useful for building confidence before eventually learning from a qualified teacher.

8. Zabihah – Find Halal Food & Prayer Spaces Anywhere

Figuring out what’s halal to eat – and where to find it – is one of the most common early challenges for new Muslims. Zabihah has been the go-to halal restaurant and market finder for decades, with one of the largest global databases in the space.

Key Features:

  • Search over 50,000 halal restaurants, markets, and butchers worldwide
  • Detailed listings with halal certification info, hours, pricing, and reviews
  • Nearby mosque and prayer space finder – especially useful when traveling
  • Community reviews and social feed for recommendations
  • Delivery links through major platforms where available

Why It’s Great for New Muslims: Adjusting to halal dietary guidelines is a major part of the transition into Islamic practice. Zabihah takes the guesswork out of finding trustworthy halal options nearby or while traveling.

9. Sunnah.com App – Authentic Hadith at Your Fingertips

Understanding the sayings and practices of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is a key part of growing in Islamic knowledge. The Sunnah.com App, built on the widely trusted Sunnah.com database, gives you direct access to major hadith collections.

Key Features:

  • Full collections including Sahih al-Bukhari, Sahih Muslim, and Sunan Abi Dawud, among others
  • Arabic and English translations side by side
  • Powerful search across collections by keyword or topic
  • Save favorite hadiths and share them easily
  • Daily hadith feature and author biographies for context

Why It’s Great for New Muslims: Beyond the Quran, hadith literature is essential for understanding how to practice Islam day to day. Having a searchable, authenticated hadith library on your phone makes it easy to look up guidance on specific topics as questions come up.

10. Muslim & Quran – Prayer Logging Made Simple

Rounding out the list is Muslim & Quran, a prayer times app with a particular focus on helping users log and review their prayer history over time.

Key Features:

  • Accurate, location-based prayer times with daylight saving time adjustment
  • PrayerBook feature to log completed prayers and view your history
  • Multiple calculation methods and Fiqh/madhab preferences
  • Customizable notification sounds for prayer alerts
  • Printable Islamic calendar and Ramadan calendar

Why It’s Great for New Muslims: Being able to look back and see your prayer consistency over weeks or months can be genuinely motivating in the early stages of building a prayer habit – turning an invisible personal effort into something you can track and reflect on.

How to Choose the Right App for You

With several solid options available, here’s a simple way to decide:

  • Want everything simplified in one place? Start with Muslims Day.
  • Want the most content-rich, globally popular option? Try Muslim Pro.
  • Want a trusted, educational-focused resource? Go with IslamicFinder.
  • Want to focus purely on building consistent prayer habits, privately? Choose The Pillars.
  • Want something simple that just handles Athan and Qibla? Go with Athan.
  • Are you a Bengali speaker? Muslim Bangla will feel the most natural and accessible.
  • Want to learn to recite and memorize the Quran? Tarteel is built exactly for that.
  • Need to find halal food or a place to pray while out? Zabihah has you covered.
  • Want to dive deeper into hadith and Islamic knowledge? Check out the Sunnah.com App.
  • Want to track your prayer history over time? Muslim & Quran makes that easy.

Many new Muslims actually use two or three apps together – for example, one focused on prayer tracking and habit-building, and another for deeper Quran study or community connection. There’s no single “correct” combination – it comes down to what helps you stay consistent.

Final Thoughts

Becoming a Muslim is a journey of learning, patience, and consistency – and the right tools can make that journey significantly smoother. Whether you choose an all-in-one Muslim lifestyle app like Muslims Day, a feature-rich option like Muslim Pro, or a language-specific app like Muslim Bangla, what matters most is finding one (or a combination) that helps you stay consistent in your daily worship.

Start simple, be patient with yourself, and let these apps support – not replace – the genuine effort of building a personal connection with your faith, one prayer at a time.
