item.title: The Story of Bahira the Monk and the Sahabi Tree: What Really Happened
item.description: Know the real story of Sahabi tree in Jordan. The 1,500-Year-Old Tree That Sheltered Prophet Muhammad ﷺ
item.content:encoded:
You must have heard the story of the tree that bowed its branches to shade a young boy, and the monk who recognized something remarkable in him – let’s discuss it again, this time in full detail.

The desert sun beat down on a slow-moving caravan making its way north from Mecca toward the trading towns of Syria. Dust rose behind camels laden with goods, and among the travelers walked a boy no older than twelve, staying close to his uncle. He had no way of knowing that this journey – and a brief encounter beneath the shade of a tree later remembered as the Sahabi Tree – would become one of the most retold stories in Islamic tradition.

This is the story of Bahira the monk, the young Muhammad ﷺ, and the ancient tree said to still stand today in the deserts of modern-day Jordan.

The Story in Brief

  • As a young boy of about 12, Muhammad ﷺ traveled with his uncle Abu Talib on a trade caravan from Mecca to Syria.
  • Along the route, near the town of Busra, the caravan rested beneath a tree now popularly known as the Sahabi Tree.
  • A Christian monk named Bahira, who lived nearby and was known for his religious knowledge, noticed unusual signs – including a cloud shading the boy and the tree bending its branches over him.
  • Bahira examined the boy and reportedly recognized signs matching descriptions of a future prophet found in older religious texts.
  • He warned Abu Talib to protect the boy carefully, particularly from those who might wish him harm, especially the Jews of that region who he feared might recognize the same signs.
  • The Sahabi Tree, still standing near Al-Karak, Jordan, is popularly associated with this event, though the historical certainty of the exact tree’s identity is debated.
  • The story itself comes from early Islamic biographical (seerah) literature, and while widely told, scholars have raised questions about certain details and the strength of its chain of narration.

Setting the Scene: A Boy Raised Under Difficult Circumstances

To understand this story, it helps to remember the circumstances of Muhammad’s ﷺ early life. He was born in Mecca around 570 CE, and by the time he was six years old, he had lost both of his parents. He was first raised by his grandfather, Abdul Muttalib, and after his grandfather’s death, his uncle Abu Talib took on the responsibility of raising him.

Abu Talib was a respected merchant, and like many in Mecca at the time, his livelihood depended on trade caravans that traveled long distances – often to Syria (Sham), a major hub of commerce in the region. When Muhammad ﷺ was around twelve years old, Abu Talib decided to take him along on one such journey, reportedly because the boy was reluctant to be separated from his uncle.

The Caravan Reaches Busra

The journey from Mecca to Syria was long, cutting through arid desert landscapes and passing through various trading towns along the way. According to the traditional account – recorded by early Islamic historians such as Ibn Ishaq and referenced in later hadith collections like Sunan al-Tirmidhi – the caravan eventually reached the outskirts of Busra, a town in what is now southern Syria, near the border of modern-day Jordan.

It was here, in this region, that the caravan is said to have stopped to rest beneath a large, shaded tree – the very tree later remembered in local tradition as the Sahabi Tree.

Nearby lived a Christian monk named Bahira, known in the area for his deep religious learning. He lived a solitary, devoted life, and travellers passing through often knew of him, though he rarely engaged much with passing caravans.

Bahira Notices Something Unusual

According to the traditional account, Bahira noticed something strange as the caravan approached and settled beneath the tree. Though he had seen countless caravans pass by over the years without paying them much attention, this time something was different.

He reportedly observed a small cloud that seemed to move and provide shade specifically over the young boy as the group traveled, and – as the caravan rested – the branches of the Sahabi Tree appeared to bend and lower themselves, extending greater shade directly over Muhammad ﷺ, even though he had settled beneath it after the others.

Intrigued and unsettled by what he was witnessing, Bahira, breaking from his usual habits, invited the entire caravan to a meal – a gesture rarely extended, and one clearly meant to give him an opportunity to observe the boy more closely.

The Examination

When the caravan arrived for the meal, Bahira reportedly noticed that the young boy had stayed behind with the belongings rather than joining the group. Sensing this was significant, he asked that no one be excluded from the invitation, and Muhammad ﷺ was brought to join them.

As the story goes, Bahira watched the boy closely throughout the gathering, and afterward, he asked Abu Talib for permission to examine him further. According to the accounts, Bahira looked for physical signs he associated with descriptions of a coming prophet found in earlier religious scriptures – reportedly including a distinctive mark between the boy’s shoulders, sometimes referred to in Islamic tradition as the “seal of prophethood.”

Bahira then asked the young boy a series of questions – about his habits, his dreams, and aspects of his daily life – and is said to have found the boy’s answers consistent with what he understood from religious texts describing a future prophet.

The Warning to Abu Talib

After completing his observations, Bahira is reported to have turned to Abu Talib with striking seriousness. He asked what relation the boy was to him, and upon learning Abu Talib was his uncle, Bahira gave him a direct and urgent piece of advice: to take the boy back home and protect him carefully, warning that if certain people – particularly some among the Jewish communities of the region who might recognize similar prophetic signs from their own scriptures – were to identify him, they might intend him harm.

Taking this warning seriously, Abu Talib is said to have shortened the trip and returned home with the boy sooner than originally planned, out of concern for his safety.

What Historians and Scholars Say

While this story is one of the most well-known accounts from the early life of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, it’s important to look at it with appropriate historical context.

The narrative appears in early seerah (biographical) literature, most notably in the work of Ibn Ishaq, one of the earliest biographers of the Prophet ﷺ, and is also referenced with some variation in later hadith collections. However, scholars of hadith have noted that certain chains of narration for this specific story contain weaknesses, and some details – particularly the more elaborate or embellished versions that developed over time – are viewed with caution by many classical and contemporary scholars.

That said, the core outline of the story – a young Muhammad ﷺ traveling to Syria with Abu Talib, and an encounter with a Christian monk who recognized something remarkable about him – is widely accepted as part of the broader historical memory of the Prophet’s ﷺ early life, even as scholars differ on the precise details and the authenticity of specific narrated elements.

This kind of nuance is common in early Islamic history – distinguishing between the general, well-attested outline of events and specific narrated details that may carry varying degrees of certainty.

The Sahabi Tree Today

Remarkably, a very old tree still stands today near Al-Karak, Jordan, popularly identified by local tradition as the same Sahabi Tree described in this story. It has become something of a local landmark, occasionally visited by travellers and those curious about early Islamic history passing through the region. However, it’s worth being clear-eyed here: while the tree is genuinely ancient and the local tradition connecting it to this story is long-standing, definitively verifying that this exact tree is the one described in 6th-century accounts is not something that can be established with certainty through historical or botanical evidence alone. It remains, more accurately, a site of strong local tradition and popular reverence rather than a scientifically confirmed historical relic.

Why This Story Still Resonates

Regardless of the exact historical details, the story of Bahira and the Sahabi Tree continues to hold meaning for Muslims as part of the broader narrative of the Prophet’s ﷺ early life – a life marked, even before prophethood formally began, by moments that those around him found remarkable and difficult to fully explain.

It also reflects an important theme found throughout Islamic tradition: the idea that signs of truth were present and recognized by sincere, knowledgeable people from other faith backgrounds – long before the message of Islam was formally revealed.

Want to Read More Stories Like This?

If stories like this – pulled from the rich history of the Prophet’s ﷺ life and the early Islamic tradition – are something you enjoy, the Muslims Day is a great place to explore more. Alongside prayer times, Quran access, and daily duas, the app features Islamic history and seerah content designed to help you connect more deeply with your faith, one story at a time.

Whether you’re a new Muslim discovering these accounts for the first time, or simply enjoy learning more about the life of the Prophet ﷺ, you’ll find more stories like this waiting inside.

[Read more stories like this on the Muslims Day Blog]

Ending Notes…

The story of Bahira the monk and the Sahabi Tree offers a glimpse into a moment long before the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ received revelation – a quiet, almost easily overlooked encounter on a dusty trade route that, in hindsight, became part of a much larger story. Whether examined as history, tradition, or an early sign pointing toward what was to come, it remains one of the most enduring and thought-provoking accounts from his early life, remembered still today beneath the shade of a tree in the Jordanian desert.

item.title: Why Is Surah Yaseen Called the ‘Heart of the Quran?
item.description: Learn the explanation of Surah Yaseen being called the heart of The Quran. Benefits of Yaseen and how to and when recite it. Learn the hadith and other reference behind claim.
item.content:encoded:
Among all 114 chapters of the Quran, few carry as much recognition and daily significance in Muslim life as Surah Yaseen. Recited after Fajr, on Friday mornings, at the bedside of the sick, and during moments of hardship, this 36th chapter of the Quran has earned a title that sets it apart from every other surah: “the Heart of the Quran.”

But where does this title actually come from? Is it based on authentic Islamic sources, and what does it really mean for a chapter of scripture to be called a “heart”? In this article, we’ll explore the origins of this title, the themes that justify it, and why Surah Yaseen continues to hold such a special place in the hearts of Muslims worldwide.

In a Nutshell

  • Surah Yaseen is referred to as the “Heart of the Quran” based on a hadith narrated in various collections, including Sunan al-Tirmidhi, though scholars differ on its authenticity.
  • The title reflects the surah’s central themes: the truth of the Quran itself, the reality of resurrection, the Oneness of Allah, and the certainty of the Hereafter – core beliefs at the very “heart” of Islamic faith.
  • Surah Yaseen is commonly recited on Friday mornings, for the sick, and at times connected to the dying or deceased, though the exact rulings vary among scholars.
  • Its poetic, rhythmic structure and emotionally powerful storytelling (like the story of the People of the Town) make it especially moving to recite and hear.
  • Whatever your reason for turning to it, Surah Yaseen remains one of the most beloved and frequently recited chapters in the Quran.

The Hadith Behind the Title

The title “Heart of the Quran” comes from a hadith attributed to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, most notably recorded in Sunan al-Tirmidhi:

“Everything has a heart, and the heart of the Quran is Yaseen. Whoever recites Yaseen, Allah records for him the reward of reciting the Quran ten times.”

This hadith is the primary basis for the widespread reputation of Surah Yaseen as holding a uniquely central place among the Quran’s chapters.

A Note on Authenticity

It’s worth being transparent here: scholars of hadith have differing opinions on the authenticity (isnad) of this particular narration. Some hadith scholars, including Imam al-Tirmidhi himself, noted weaknesses in the chain of narrators. Others, like certain later scholars, considered supporting narrations strong enough to accept the general meaning.

Regardless of the debate around this specific hadith’s grading, the sentiment behind it – that Surah Yaseen holds exceptional thematic and spiritual weight – is widely accepted across the Muslim world, reflected in centuries of consistent practice and reverence for this chapter.

Why “Heart”? Understanding the Metaphor

To understand why Surah Yaseen earned this title, it helps to think about what a heart actually does. The heart is the center of the body – it pumps life to every other organ, and without it, nothing else functions. In the same way, the themes covered in Surah Yaseen represent the core, life-giving beliefs at the center of Islamic faith.

The surah touches on:

  1. The truth and divine origin of the Quran itself
  2. The Oneness of Allah (Tawheed)
  3. The certainty of resurrection and the Hereafter
  4. The consequences of belief versus disbelief
  5. Allah’s power over creation, life, and death

These aren’t peripheral topics – they are the foundational pillars of Islamic belief. Just as a physical heart sustains the entire body, these core beliefs sustain a Muslim’s entire worldview and practice.

Key Themes of Surah Yaseen

1. Affirming the Prophethood and the Quran’s Truth

The surah opens by affirming that the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is indeed a messenger sent with truth, on a “straight path.” This sets the tone for everything that follows – establishing the divine authority behind the message being delivered.

2. The Story of the People of the Town (Ashab al-Qaryah)

One of the most powerful narratives in Surah Yaseen is the story of a town whose people rejected three messengers sent to guide them. A man from the outskirts of the city came running to defend the messengers and call his people to belief – even as he faced rejection and, ultimately, martyrdom. Despite this, his final words reflect no bitterness, only hope that his people would come to understand the truth he had embraced.

This story is a powerful lesson in sincerity, steadfastness in faith, and the tragic consequences of rejecting truth out of arrogance or stubbornness.

3. Signs of Allah in Creation

The surah draws attention to signs of Allah’s power throughout the natural world – the revival of dead land through rain, the alternation of day and night, the sun and moon each following their precise orbits, and the miracle of human reproduction and growth. These verses invite deep reflection (tafakkur) on the order and design present in creation.

4. The Reality of Resurrection

Perhaps the most emphasized theme in Surah Yaseen is the certainty of resurrection and the Day of Judgment. The surah directly addresses the disbelievers’ doubt about how decayed bones could ever be brought back to life, responding with a powerful rhetorical argument: the same God who created humans from nothing the first time is more than capable of recreating them.

“Does man not consider that We created him from a [mere] sperm-drop – then, at once, he is a clear opponent [of Allah]? And he presents for Us an example, forgetting his own creation. He says, ‘Who will give life to bones while they are disintegrated?’ Say, ‘He will give them life who produced them the first time…'” (paraphrased summary of Surah Yaseen, verses 77–79)

This section serves as one of the clearest and most compelling arguments for resurrection found anywhere in the Quran – reinforcing why this surah is seen as touching the very “heart” of Islamic belief.

5. The Final Warning and Allah’s Complete Power

The surah closes with a powerful reminder of Allah’s absolute command over all things: “When He intends a thing, His command is only that He says to it, ‘Be,’ and it is.” This final note reinforces the central theme running throughout – total submission to, and trust in, the power and wisdom of Allah.

Common Occasions for Reciting Surah Yaseen

Because of its central themes and the hadith describing its virtue, Surah Yaseen is recited in a variety of contexts across Muslim communities worldwide:

  • On Friday mornings – a widely practiced tradition in many communities, though scholars differ on whether this is a specifically established Sunnah or a beneficial general practice.
  • For those who are ill – many recite it while visiting or praying for someone who is sick, drawing on its themes of Allah’s power over life and healing.
  • Near the time of death or for the deceased – this is a widely discussed practice; while some hadiths reference reciting it near the dying, scholars have varying opinions on the authenticity and specific application of these narrations, so practices differ between communities and schools of thought.
  • During times of hardship or seeking barakah (blessing) – many Muslims turn to Surah Yaseen generally for comfort, reflection, and spiritual connection.

Given the range of scholarly opinion on some of these specific occasions, it’s always encouraged to consult a knowledgeable local scholar regarding practices you’re unfamiliar with.

The Literary and Emotional Power of Surah Yaseen

Beyond its theological themes, Surah Yaseen is also recognized for its beautiful literary structure. Its verses often end with rhythmic, rhyming patterns typical of the Meccan surahs, giving it a poetic, flowing quality when recited aloud. This rhythmic beauty, combined with emotionally resonant storytelling – particularly the account of the believing man in the story of the town – contributes to why so many Muslims find this surah especially moving to listen to and recite.

For many, the experience of hearing Surah Yaseen recited by a skilled reciter is not just an intellectual exercise but a deeply emotional and spiritual one – reinforcing, once again, why it’s so fittingly compared to a “heart.”

Reflecting on Surah Yaseen in Daily Life

Understanding why Surah Yaseen is called the “Heart of the Quran” isn’t just an academic exercise – it’s an invitation to engage with the surah more deeply. Rather than reciting it purely out of habit or tradition, taking time to reflect on its themes – the certainty of resurrection, the signs of Allah in creation, and the story of sincere faith in the face of rejection – can transform the experience of recitation into something genuinely heart-cantered.

item.title: Qibla Compass vs GPS-Based Qibla Finder: Which Is More Accurate?
item.description: Get to know the real differences between the Qibla finder; traditional and digital ones. How technologies make life easier to find qibla direction.
item.content:encoded:
Every Muslim knows the importance of facing the Qibla – the direction of the Kaaba in Mecca – during prayer. But when it comes to actually finding that direction, especially when traveling or in an unfamiliar location, two main tools dominate: the traditional Qibla compass and the modern GPS-based Qibla finder built into most smartphone apps.

At first glance, they might seem interchangeable – both point you toward Mecca. But under the hood, they work in fundamentally different ways, and each comes with its own strengths, weaknesses, and potential sources of error. In this guide, we’ll break down exactly how each method works, where accuracy problems commonly arise, and which option is genuinely more reliable for your daily prayers.

Quick Answer Before You Dive In

  • A traditional Qibla compass relies on Earth’s magnetic field and requires manual adjustment for magnetic declination – it can be accurate, but only if used correctly and away from magnetic interference.
  • A GPS-based Qibla finder (used in most smartphone apps) combines your phone’s GPS location with digital compass sensors to automatically calculate and display the Qibla direction – generally more convenient and often more accurate for everyday use.
  • The biggest sources of error for both methods are magnetic interference (metal objects, electronics, buildings) and poor calibration – not the underlying technology itself.
  • For most people, a well-calibrated GPS-based Qibla finder app offers the best balance of accuracy and convenience, especially while traveling.
  • A physical Qibla compass remains useful as a reliable backup, particularly in areas with poor GPS signal or during travel to remote locations.

How a Traditional Qibla Compass Works

A traditional Qibla compass functions much like a standard magnetic compass, with one key difference: it includes a pre-marked scale or dial indicating the Qibla direction for a specific location or requires the user to manually calculate and set the correct bearing.

The Basic Mechanism

At its core, a magnetic compass uses a magnetized needle that aligns itself with Earth’s magnetic field, pointing toward magnetic north. Once you know magnetic north, you can calculate the direction to the Kaaba by knowing the Qibla bearing (in degrees) for your specific location.

Why This Requires Extra Steps

Here’s where it gets more complex: Earth’s magnetic north pole is not the same as true north (the geographic North Pole used in Qibla bearing calculations). The difference between the two is called magnetic declination, and it varies depending on where you are in the world – sometimes by a significant number of degrees.

To use a traditional Qibla compass accurately, you generally need to:

  1. Know the correct Qibla bearing (in degrees from true north) for your specific city or coordinates
  2. Know the magnetic declination for your location
  3. Manually adjust the compass reading to account for that declination
  4. Ensure the compass is held flat and away from magnetic interference

Common Sources of Error

Traditional compasses are highly sensitive to magnetic interference. Accuracy can be thrown off by:

  • Nearby metal objects (belt buckles, phones, jewelry, furniture with metal frames)
  • Electronic devices and appliances
  • Structural steel in buildings (especially in high-rise apartments or offices)
  • Vehicles, when used inside or near a car
  • Failing to account for magnetic declination correctly

Because of these factors, a traditional Qibla compass – while simple and battery-free – requires a fair amount of user knowledge and care to use correctly.

How a GPS-Based Qibla Finder Works

A GPS-based Qibla finder, the kind built into most Islamic lifestyle apps, works quite differently. Instead of relying purely on magnetic north and manual calculations, it combines multiple data sources to automatically calculate and display your Qibla direction in real time.

The Technology Behind It

GPS-based Qibla finders typically use a combination of:

  1. GPS location data – to determine your exact latitude and longitude
  2. Great-circle calculation – the app calculates the shortest path (great-circle bearing) from your coordinates to the Kaaba’s coordinates (21.4225° N, 39.8262° E)
  3. Digital compass (magnetometer) sensor – built into your smartphone, used to detect your phone’s current orientation
  4. Automatic declination correction – many apps automatically factor in magnetic declination for your location, removing the need for manual calculation

The result is typically a live, rotating arrow or compass display that updates as you move your phone, pointing you directly toward the Qibla without requiring you to do any manual math.

Common Sources of Error

Despite being more automated, GPS-based Qibla finders aren’t immune to accuracy issues either:

  • Uncalibrated magnetometer – smartphone compass sensors can drift and need periodic recalibration (usually done by moving the phone in a figure-8 motion)
  • Magnetic interference – just like traditional compasses, phone sensors are affected by nearby metal, magnets, and electronics (including phone cases with magnetic clasps)
  • Weak GPS signal – indoors or in dense urban areas, GPS accuracy can degrade, throwing off the location-based calculation
  • Software/calculation differences – not all apps use the same calculation method, and low-quality apps may use simplified or less accurate formulas

Head-to-Head: Qibla Compass vs GPS-Based Qibla Finder

So, Which One Is Actually More Accurate?

The honest answer: it depends less on the technology itself and more on how correctly it’s used and calibrated.

When a Traditional Qibla Compass Wins

  • In areas with no GPS signal, no internet, or no charged device available
  • For users who understand magnetic declination and can apply it correctly
  • As a reliable backup tool that doesn’t depend on battery life

When a GPS-Based Qibla Finder Wins

  • For everyday convenience, especially while traveling to new cities or countries
  • For users who don’t want to manually calculate declination or bearings
  • When using a well-reviewed, reputable app that handles declination correction automatically
  • In most modern smartphones, which now have reasonably accurate GPS and magnetometer sensors when properly calibrated

For the average person praying at home, work, or while traveling, a GPS-based Qibla finder from a trusted app is generally the more practical and accurate option – provided the phone’s compass sensor is properly calibrated and used away from magnetic interference.

That said, a physical Qibla compass still holds real value as a dependable backup – particularly for travelers heading to remote areas, hikers, or anyone who wants a tool that doesn’t rely on battery power or a data connection.

Tips for Getting the Most Accurate Reading (Either Method)

Regardless of which tool you use, these tips will significantly improve accuracy:

  1. Move away from metal and electronics – step away from tables with metal legs, other phones, laptops, and speakers before checking direction.
  2. Calibrate your phone’s compass regularly – most Qibla apps have a calibration feature (often a figure-8 motion) – use it, especially if the reading seems off.
  3. Hold the device flat and level – tilting your phone or compass can throw off the reading.
  4. Double-check with a known reference – if you’re at home, once you find the Qibla direction, mark it physically (e.g., with a sticker or by noting a fixed point in the room) so you don’t need to recheck every time.
  5. Use a reputable app – not all Qibla finder apps use the same calculation accuracy; stick with well-reviewed, established apps.
  6. When indoors, get near a window if possible – this can improve GPS signal accuracy before locking in your direction.

A Simple Rule of Thumb

If you’re at home and pray in the same spot regularly, it’s worth taking a few extra minutes to verify your Qibla direction carefully – using either a well-calibrated GPS-based Qibla finder or a correctly adjusted traditional compass – and then marking that direction permanently in your prayer space. This removes the need to rely on real-time readings (and their potential for error) every single time you pray.

For travel, hotel rooms, or unfamiliar locations, a GPS-based Qibla finder app offers the fastest and generally most reliable way to get an accurate direction on the spot.

Find Your Qibla Direction Instantly With Muslims Day

Getting your Qibla direction right is just one small part of building a consistent, confident prayer routine — and having the right tools in one place makes a real difference. The Muslims Day App has a dedicated Qibla compass feature built right in, using GPS-based calculation to point you accurately toward the Kaaba, wherever you are — no manual adjustments, no guesswork.

Alongside the compass, the app also includes accurate prayer time notifications, Quran access, and daily duas, making it a complete companion for your daily prayer routine.

Whether you’re praying at home or figuring out your direction on the road, the Qibla compass feature inside Muslims Day is designed to stay accurate and easy to use.

Final Thoughts

Both the traditional Qibla compass and modern GPS-based Qibla finders can point you accurately toward the Kaaba – but each comes with its own requirements for correct use. A traditional compass demands manual knowledge of magnetic declination and careful handling, while a GPS-based finder offers convenience and automation, provided your device is properly calibrated and free from magnetic interference.

For most people today, a reliable GPS-based Qibla finder app offers the best combination of accuracy and ease of use – while a physical compass remains a smart backup for situations where technology isn’t an option. Understanding how each tool works – and where they can go wrong – is the real key to consistently facing the Qibla with confidence.

item.title: Short vs Long Dua Qunoot: Different Versions Explained
item.description: Learn the explanation of short vs long dua qunoot. Learn the benefits of dua qunoot and when to perform it.
item.content:encoded:
If you’ve ever prayed Witr behind different imams, you may have noticed something: the Dua Qunoot they recite isn’t always the same length. Sometimes it’s a short, simple supplication lasting a few seconds. Other times, it’s a longer, more elaborate dua that continues for a minute or more.

This isn’t a mistake or inconsistency – it reflects genuine, authentic variations in how Dua Qunoot has been transmitted and practiced across different scholarly traditions. In this guide, we’ll break down the short and long versions of Dua Qunoot, where each comes from, and when each is typically used.

💡 Quick Tip: Want both versions of Dua Qunoot saved for easy access during Witr prayer? The Muslims Day App includes the full Arabic text, transliteration, and translation for both the short and long Dua Qunoot – so you can review or memorize it anytime. [Explore Muslims Day App

Quick Summary

  • Dua Qunoot is a supplication recited in the Witr prayer, typically in the final rak’ah after ruku (bowing) or before it, depending on the school of thought.
  • The short Dua Qunoot is the version taught by the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ to his grandson Hasan ibn Ali, and is the most widely authenticated and commonly used version.
  • The long Dua Qunoot includes additional lines of praise and supplication, drawn from various companions’ practices, and is more commonly used in certain regions and by scholars who prefer a more extended recitation.
  • Both versions are valid; the choice often comes down to madhab (school of thought), regional tradition, or personal preference within permissible limits.
  • There’s also a separate concept called Qunoot al-Nazilah – a special Dua Qunoot recited during times of calamity or hardship, distinct from the regular Witr qunoot.

What Is Dua Qunoot?

Dua Qunoot (دعاء القنوت) is a specific supplication recited by Muslims, most commonly during the Witr prayer – an odd-numbered prayer performed after Isha and considered highly recommended (sunnah mu’akkadah) in Islam.

The word “Qunoot” linguistically refers to devotion, obedience, and standing in humble submission before Allah. In practice, it refers to this specific dua recited while standing during prayer, usually in the last rak’ah of Witr.

The Short Dua Qunoot

Origin

The short version of Dua Qunoot is the most authentically documented and widely recited across the Muslim world. It was taught directly by the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ to his grandson, Hasan ibn Ali (RA), who narrated:

“The Messenger of Allah ﷺ taught me some words to say in the Witr prayer…” (Recorded in Sunan Abu Dawood, At-Tirmidhi, and other hadith collections)

Because of this strong and direct chain of transmission, the short Dua Qunoot is considered the most authentic and is the version most commonly taught in Islamic schools, mosques, and Quran memorization programs worldwide.

The Short Dua Qunoot (Arabic)

اللَّهُمَّ اهْدِنِي فِيمَنْ هَدَيْتَ، وَعَافِنِي فِيمَنْ عَافَيْتَ، وَتَوَلَّنِي فِيمَنْ تَوَلَّيْتَ، وَبَارِكْ لِي فِيمَا أَعْطَيْتَ، وَقِنِي شَرَّ مَا قَضَيْتَ، فَإِنَّكَ تَقْضِي وَلَا يُقْضَى عَلَيْكَ، وَإِنَّهُ لَا يَذِلُّ مَنْ وَالَيْتَ، تَبَارَكْتَ رَبَّنَا وَتَعَالَيْتَ

Transliteration

“Allahumma-hdini feeman hadayt, wa ‘aafini feeman ‘aafayt, wa tawallani feeman tawallayt, wa baarik lee feema a’tayt, wa qini sharra ma qadayt, fa innaka taqdi wa la yuqda ‘alayk, wa innahu la yadhillu man walayt, tabarakta rabbana wa ta’aalayt.”

English Translation

“O Allah, guide me among those You have guided, pardon me among those You have pardoned, turn to me in friendship among those on whom You have turned in friendship, and bless me in what You have bestowed, and save me from the evil of what You have decreed. For verily You decree, and none can decree against You. He whom You befriend is not humiliated. Blessed are You, our Lord, and Exalted.”

When It’s Used

This short version is used by the majority of Muslims globally during Witr prayer and is often the first version taught to children and new Muslims due to its brevity and strong authenticity.

[IMAGE PLACEHOLDER 3 – Short Dua Qunoot] Prompt: A minimalist illustration of an open prayer book with Arabic calligraphy, soft candlelight, warm and peaceful tone, symbolic representation of memorization and learning

The Long Dua Qunoot

Origin

The longer version of Dua Qunoot incorporates additional lines of praise, glorification, and supplication beyond the short version. It draws from various narrations attributed to companions such as Umar ibn al-Khattab (RA) and is commonly associated with certain regional and scholarly traditions, particularly within parts of the Hanafi madhab and some South Asian and Middle Eastern communities.

This version is longer not because it replaces the short one, but because certain traditions add extra supplications – often including additional praise of Allah, seeking forgiveness, and sending blessings upon the Prophet ﷺ – either combined with the short version or recited separately.

A Common Extended Addition

Many who recite the long Dua Qunoot include this additional portion after (or alongside) the short version:

اللَّهُمَّ إِنَّا نَسْتَعِينُكَ وَنَسْتَغْفِرُكَ وَنُثْنِي عَلَيْكَ الْخَيْرَ وَلَا نَكْفُرُكَ وَنَخْلَعُ وَنَتْرُكُ مَنْ يَفْجُرُكَ، اللَّهُمَّ إِيَّاكَ نَعْبُدُ وَلَكَ نُصَلِّي وَنَسْجُدُ وَإِلَيْكَ نَسْعَى وَنَحْفِدُ، نَرْجُو رَحْمَتَكَ وَنَخْشَى عَذَابَكَ، إِنَّ عَذَابَكَ الْجِدَّ بِالْكُفَّارِ مُلْحِقٌ

Transliteration:

“Allahumma inna nasta’eenuka wa nastaghfiruka wa nuthni ‘alaykal-khayr wa la nakfuruka wa nakhla’u wa natruku man yafjuruk. Allahumma iyyaka na’budu wa laka nusalli wa nasjudu wa ilayka nas’aa wa nahfid, narju rahmataka wa nakhsha ‘adhabaka, inna ‘adhabakal-jidda bil kuffari mulhiq.”

English Translation (summary):

“O Allah, we seek Your help, seek Your forgiveness, and praise You with all goodness. We do not disbelieve in You, and we forsake and abandon whoever disobeys You. O Allah, You alone we worship, to You we pray and prostrate, and to You we hasten to serve. We hope for Your mercy and fear Your punishment, for indeed Your punishment will surely reach the disbelievers.”

When It’s Used

The long version of Dua Qunoot tends to be more common in specific regional practices and among those following certain scholarly interpretations. It’s often recited by imams in congregational Witr prayers, particularly during Ramadan, when Witr is prayed in congregation after Taraweeh.

Short vs Long Dua Qunoot: Key Differences

Both versions are considered valid within Islamic practice, and the difference largely comes down to regional custom, madhab preference, and the setting (individual prayer vs. congregational prayer led by an imam).

Qunoot al-Nazilah: A Special Category

It’s worth briefly distinguishing regular Dua Qunoot from Qunoot al-Nazilah – a special supplication recited during times of severe hardship, calamity, war, or crisis affecting the Muslim community. Unlike the regular Witr qunoot, Qunoot al-Nazilah:

  • Can be recited in any of the five daily prayers, not just Witr
  • Is typically recited after rising from ruku in the final rak’ah
  • Often includes specific supplications relevant to the crisis at hand (e.g., praying for the oppressed, for safety, for relief from hardship)

This is a separate practice from the everyday Dua Qunoot discussed above, though both share the same root concept of standing in humble supplication.

Which Version Should You Recite?

There is no single “correct” answer – this often depends on:

  1. Your madhab or regional tradition – if you follow a particular school of thought or community practice, it’s generally best to follow what’s taught by your local scholars or mosque.
  2. The setting – many people use the short version for personal, individual Witr prayer and reserve the long version (or a combination) for congregational prayer, especially during Ramadan.
  3. Personal comfort and memorization – beginners are often encouraged to start with the short, well-authenticated version before gradually learning the longer one if desired.

Ultimately, both the short and long Dua Qunoot are rooted in authentic Islamic tradition, and reciting either with sincerity and understanding is what matters most – not the length.

Tips for Memorizing Dua Qunoot

  • Break it into small phrases – memorize a few words at a time rather than the whole dua at once.
  • Understand the meaning – knowing what you’re saying makes memorization more meaningful and long-lasting.
  • Practice during non-prayer times first – repeat it during the day before trying to recite it confidently in Witr.
  • Listen to correct recitation – hearing a qualified reciter helps with pronunciation and rhythm.
  • Be consistent – reciting it nightly during Witr naturally reinforces memorization over time.

Keep Dua Qunoot Close, Anytime You Need It

Whether you’re praying individually or preparing to lead Witr in congregation, Muslims Day App helps you stay consistent and confident in your daily worship.

Final Thoughts

The existence of both short and long versions of Dua Qunoot reflects the richness and flexibility within Islamic scholarly tradition – not confusion or contradiction. Whether you recite the short, widely-authenticated version taught to Hasan ibn Ali, or the longer version common in congregational and Ramadan prayers, what matters most is approaching it with sincerity, humility, and a genuine desire to seek Allah’s guidance and mercy.

Take time to learn the version most relevant to your community and tradition, understand its meaning, and let it become a consistent, heartfelt part of your Witr prayer.

item.title: When Was the Quran Written? A Complete Timeline From Revelation to Compilation
item.description: Learn the history of When Was the Quran Written. Timeframe and date by date history has been showcased. A perfect guide for readers who want to know true history of Quran.
item.content:encoded:
For over 1,400 years, the Quran has remained the central text of Islam, guiding the beliefs, practices, and daily lives of more than a billion Muslims worldwide. But one question that comes up often-especially among new Muslims, students of religion, and curious non-Muslims-is: when was the Quran actually written?

The answer isn’t a single date. It’s a journey-one that spans revelation, memorization, oral transmission, and eventual compilation into the written text we know today. This article breaks down that entire process in a clear, chronological timeline.

The Quran Was Revealed, Not “Written” All at Once

Before diving into the timeline, it’s important to understand a key distinction: the Quran was not authored in the way a book is typically written. Muslims believe it is the literal word of God (Allah), revealed to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ through the angel Jibril (Gabriel) over a period of approximately 23 years.

This revelation happened gradually-in response to events, questions, and circumstances the early Muslim community faced-rather than being delivered as one complete manuscript.

Complete Timeline: From First Revelation to Final Compilation

610 CE-The First Revelation in the Cave of Hira

The story begins when Muhammad ﷺ, then 40 years old, was meditating in the Cave of Hira, located on Jabal al-Nour (“Mountain of Light”) near Mecca. It was here that the Angel Jibril appeared to him and delivered the first verses of the Quran, found in Surah Al-Alaq (96:1-5), beginning with the word “Iqra” (“Read” or “Recite”).

This moment marks the beginning of Prophethood and the start of the Quran’s revelation.

610–622 CE-The Meccan Period

For the next 13 years, while still in Mecca, the Prophet ﷺ continued receiving revelations. These early chapters (surahs) tend to be shorter, poetic in style, and focus heavily on core beliefs: the Oneness of God (Tawheed), the Day of Judgment, moral conduct, and stories of earlier prophets.

622 CE-The Hijrah (Migration to Medina)

A turning point occurs with the Hijrah-the migration of the Prophet ﷺ and his followers from Mecca to Medina. This event is so significant that it marks the start of the Islamic (Hijri) calendar.

622–632 CE-The Medinan Period

Once in Medina, the nature of the revelations shifted. Medinan surahs tend to be longer and more detailed, addressing social laws, family matters, governance, warfare ethics, and community organization-reflecting the new responsibilities of building an actual Muslim society and state.

During the Prophet’s Lifetime-Oral Preservation and Early Writing

Throughout these 23 years, the Quran was preserved in two parallel ways:

  1. Memorization (Hifz): Companions of the Prophet ﷺ memorized the verses as they were revealed. Many companions, known as Huffaz (memorizers), could recite large portions-or the entire Quran-from memory.
  2. Written Recording: The Prophet ﷺ appointed scribes, most notably Zayd ibn Thabit, to write down verses as they were revealed. These were recorded on whatever materials were available at the time-parchment, flat stones, palm leaves, leather, and even animal bones and shoulder blades.

Importantly, this dual system-memorization plus writing-meant the Quran was never dependent on a single copy or a single person’s memory. This redundancy became crucial in the years following the Prophet’s death.

632 CE-The Death of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ

By the time of his death, the entire Quran had been revealed and existed in two forms: memorized by numerous companions and written down in scattered pieces by various scribes. However, it had not yet been compiled into a single, bound book.

The Compilation of the Quran Into a Single Text

632–634 CE-Caliph Abu Bakr’s Compilation

After the Prophet’s death, Abu Bakr became the first Caliph (leader of the Muslim community). During his rule, a serious challenge arose: the Battle of Yamama, in which a significant number of Huffaz (Quran memorizers) were killed.

This loss alarmed the companion Umar ibn al-Khattab, who urged Abu Bakr to organize a formal, complete written compilation of the Quran to safeguard it against loss. Abu Bakr assigned this task to Zayd ibn Thabit, who had been one of the Prophet’s primary scribes.

Zayd meticulously cross-referenced written fragments with the memories of multiple Huffaz to compile a single, authenticated manuscript. This became known as the Mushaf-the first complete written copy of the Quran as one unified text.

644–656 CE-Caliph Uthman ibn Affan’s Standardization

As Islam spread rapidly beyond Arabia into Persia, Syria, Egypt, and beyond, regional dialectical differences in recitation began causing confusion and, in some cases, disputes among new Muslim communities about the “correct” pronunciation and reading of the Quran.

To resolve this, the third Caliph, Uthman ibn Affan, ordered the creation of standardized copies of the Quran based on Abu Bakr’s original Mushaf. He formed a committee-again led by Zayd ibn Thabit-to produce several official copies written in the Quraysh dialect (the Prophet’s own dialect), which was considered the most authoritative.

These standardized copies, known as the Uthmanic codices, were sent to major Islamic centers such as Mecca, Kufa, Basra, and Damascus. All other variant manuscripts were ordered to be destroyed to prevent future discrepancies.

This Uthmanic text became the single, standardized version of the Quran that is used by Muslims worldwide today-essentially unchanged for nearly 1,400 years.

Quick Reference Timeline

Why This Timeline Matters

Understanding “When Was the Quran Written” is a common misconception-that the Quran was written like an ordinary book, by one person, at one point in time. In reality, it reflects a careful, deliberate process of revelation over 23 years, followed by preservation through both memory and writing, and finally, formal compilation to ensure its accuracy would endure for generations.

Muslims believe this process, combined with the unbroken chain of memorization (Hifz) that continues to this day, is part of what has preserved the Quran’s text unchanged since the 7th century-a claim rooted in the Quranic verse:

“Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder [the Quran], and indeed, We will be its guardian.” (Surah Al-Hijr, 15:9)

Final Thoughts

The Quran’s journey-from a single revelation in a quiet cave outside Mecca to a fully standardized text distributed across a growing Islamic world-is a story of preservation, dedication, and continuity. While the revelation itself spanned 23 years (610–632 CE), the process of transforming it into the written, compiled text we recognize today took a few more decades, concluding under Caliph Uthman around 650 CE.

For Muslims, this history isn’t just academic-it’s a testament to the care taken to protect the words believed to be directly from God, ensuring they remain accessible and unaltered for every generation that follows.

item.content:encoded:
Life is full of crossroads-choosing a spouse, accepting a job offers, moving to a new city, starting a business, or deciding between two equally good options. For Muslims, one of the most beautiful tools given by the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ to navigate these moments of uncertainty is Istikhara-the prayer for seeking Allah’s guidance.

Unlike relying purely on logic, advice from others, or gut feeling, Istikhara is a spiritual practice rooted in humility: it’s an acknowledgment that Allah knows what is best for us, even when we don’t. In this guide, we’ll explore what Istikhara really means, when to perform it, the exact dua and method, and how to understand the outcome.

💡 Tip: Want the Istikhara dua, prayer times, and daily reminders in one place? The Muslims Day App keeps the full Istikhara dua (Arabic, transliteration, and translation), prayer time alerts, and Qibla direction right on your phone-so you’re never searching for it when you need it most.

What Is Istikhara?

The word Istikhara comes from the Arabic root khayr, meaning “good” or “goodness.” Literally, it means “seeking the good” or “asking Allah to choose the best option.”

Istikhara is a specific prayer (Salatul Istikhara) combined with a dua, taught directly by the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ to his companions. It is performed when a person is unsure about a decision and wants to place their trust in Allah’s wisdom rather than relying solely on their own limited judgment.

The Prophet ﷺ used to teach his companions the method of Istikhara for all matters, just as he would teach them a chapter of the Quran-showing how seriously this practice was regarded (Sahih al-Bukhari).

Why Istikhara Matters in Islam

Human beings are often blind to the long-term consequences of their choices. A job that looks perfect today might bring hardship later. A relationship that seems ideal might not be spiritually or emotionally healthy. Istikhara is rooted in the belief that:

  • Allah has complete knowledge of the past, present, and future.
  • What may seem good to us might not truly be good for us-and vice versa.
  • True contentment comes from trusting that Allah will guide us toward what is best, even if it doesn’t match our initial preference.

This concept is beautifully reflected in the Quran:

“But perhaps you hate a thing and it is good for you; and perhaps you love a thing and it is bad for you. And Allah Knows, while you know not.” (Surah Al-Baqarah, 2:216)

When Should You Perform Istikhara?

Istikhara can be performed for any decision, big or small, where you feel uncertain about the right path. Common situations include:

  • Marriage proposals-deciding whether to accept or move forward with a potential spouse
  • Career or job decisions-accepting a new job, changing careers, or starting a business
  • Relocation-moving to a new city or country
  • Education choices-selecting a university, course, or field of study
  • Major purchases-buying a house, car, or making significant investments
  • Any situation with two or more permissible options where you’re unsure which is best

It’s important to note: Istikhara should only be used for matters that are halal (permissible). It is not meant to be used to seek guidance on something already forbidden in Islam-for example, one wouldn’t perform Istikhara to decide whether to engage in something sinful.

When NOT to Perform Istikhara

Istikhara is unnecessary for:

  • Obligatory acts of worship (e.g., you don’t need Istikhara to decide whether to pray five times a day-it’s already required).
  • Clearly prohibited actions (e.g., you wouldn’t seek guidance on whether to consume something haram).

It is specifically designed for situations of genuine, permissible uncertainty.

How to Perform Salatul Istikhara: Step-by-Step

Step 1: Perform Wudu (Ablution)

As with any prayer, begin by performing wudu to ensure physical and spiritual purity.

Step 2: Pray Two Rak’ahs (Optional Prayer)

Perform two units (rak’ahs) of voluntary (nafl) prayer, separate from your obligatory prayers. This can be done at any time except during the specifically prohibited times for prayer (immediately after Fajr, at midday, and immediately after Asr).

In these two rak’ahs, it’s recommended (though not obligatory) to recite:

  • Surah Al-Kafirun (Chapter 109) in the first rak’ah after Al-Fatiha
  • Surah Al-Ikhlas (Chapter 112) in the second rak’ah after Al-Fatiha

Step 3: Recite the Istikhara Dua

After completing the two rak’ahs, while still in a state of reflection, recite the dua of Istikhara. It’s recommended to have the specific matter or decision in mind (or mention it silently/verbally) while making this dua.

The Istikhara Dua (Arabic):

اللَّهُمَّ إِنِّي أَسْتَخِيرُكَ بِعِلْمِكَ، وَأَسْتَقْدِرُكَ بِقُدْرَتِكَ، وَأَسْأَلُكَ مِنْ فَضْلِكَ الْعَظِيمِ، فَإِنَّكَ تَقْدِرُ وَلَا أَقْدِرُ، وَتَعْلَمُ وَلَا أَعْلَمُ، وَأَنْتَ عَلَّامُ الْغُيُوبِ

Transliteration:

“Allahumma inni astakhiruka bi’ilmika, wa astaqdiruka bi qudratika, wa as’aluka min fadlika al-‘azeem, fa innaka taqdiru wa la aqdiru, wa ta’lamu wa la a’lamu, wa anta ‘allamul-ghuyub.”

English Translation:

“O Allah, I seek Your guidance [in making a choice] by virtue of Your knowledge, and I seek ability by virtue of Your power, and I ask You of Your great bounty. You have power, I have none. And You know, I know not. You are the Knower of hidden things.”

Step 4: Mention Your Specific Matter

After this, the Prophet ﷺ taught that a person should mention their specific situation by name. For example, if deciding on a job offer, one might say (in Arabic or their own language):

“O Allah, if you know that this matter-[mention job/marriage/decision]-is good for me in my religion, my livelihood, and the outcome of my affairs (or: in this world and the next), then decree it for me, make it easy for me, and bless me in it. But if You know that this matter is bad for me in my religion, my livelihood, and the outcome of my affairs, then turn it away from me, and turn me away from it, and decree for me what is good wherever it may be and make me content with it.”

What Happens After Istikhara? Understanding the Signs

This is one of the most commonly misunderstood aspects of Istikhara. Many people expect a dream, a clear “yes” or “no” sign, or some dramatic spiritual experience immediately after praying. However, this is not a requirement or guarantee.

Common Misconceptions

  • Myth: You must see a dream after Istikhara. Reality: While some people do report dreams, this is not the primary or required mechanism through which Allah answers Istikhara. Many scholars emphasize that dreams are not the main sign to rely on.
  • Myth: You’ll instantly know the “right” choice through a strong feeling. Reality: Sometimes yes, but often the answer to Istikhara unfolds gradually-through circumstances, ease or difficulty in pursuing the matter, a growing sense of clarity, or even a change of heart over time.

How the Answer Actually Unfolds

Most scholars agree that Allah answers Istikhara through the natural course of events following the prayer:

  1. Ease or difficulty-If a path becomes smooth, opportunities align, and things fall into place without excessive struggle, this can be a sign of it being the right choice.
  2. Obstacles and closed doors-If a matter becomes increasingly difficult, or falls apart despite genuine effort, this may indicate it isn’t the best path.
  3. Inner peace (sakeenah)-A sense of contentment and ease in the heart about the decision, even if it wasn’t the initially preferred option.
  4. Consultation (Shura)-Istikhara doesn’t replace practical steps. It’s recommended to also consult trusted, knowledgeable people (family, mentors, scholars) alongside performing Istikhara.

Can You Repeat Istikhara?

Yes. If a person remains uncertain after performing Istikhara once, they are encouraged to repeat it-even multiple times over several days-until they feel a sense of clarity or peace about the decision. There is no fixed limit on how many times it can be performed.

Practical Tips for Performing Istikhara Sincerely

  • Have sincere intention (niyyah): Approach Istikhara with genuine willingness to accept whatever outcome Allah decrees, not just seeking confirmation of what you already want.
  • Let go of attachment to a specific outcome: True Istikhara requires openness to either result-proceeding or stepping back.
  • Pair it with dua and patience: Guidance often unfolds over time, not instantly.
  • Don’t skip practical steps: Research, seek advice, and use sound judgment alongside your prayer-Istikhara complements human effort, it doesn’t replace it.
  • Trust the process: Even if the outcome isn’t what you initially hoped for, trust that Allah’s decree carries wisdom beyond what we can see.

A Note on Emotional Well-Being During Big Decisions

Major life decisions-especially around marriage, career changes, or relocation-can bring real stress and anxiety. Istikhara offers a spiritual anchor during these times, but it’s also completely normal to feel uncertain or emotionally overwhelmed while waiting for clarity. Combining istikhara with patience, self-care, and honest conversations with people you trust can make the process feel less isolating.

Final Thoughts

Istikhara is more than a ritual-it’s a mindset. It teaches Muslims to approach life’s uncertainties with humility, patience, and trust in Allah’s infinite wisdom. Whether you’re facing a decision about marriage, career, or any other significant life choice, performing Istikhara sincerely- followed by careful thought, consultation, and patience-can bring genuine peace of mind.

The goal isn’t to receive a dramatic sign, but to align your heart with acceptance: trusting that whatever unfolds, whether it’s the outcome you hoped for or not, is ultimately what is best for you-in this life and the next.
